base.name: overview
base.description: The design system is built to be AI-friendly: consistent naming, predictable prop patterns, and a CLI that feeds structured documentation directly into AI context windows. But models still need the right context to avoid falling back to…
prose: Overview

The design system is built to be AI-friendly: consistent naming, predictable prop patterns, and a CLI that feeds structured documentation directly into AI context windows. But models still need the right context to avoid falling back to generic React patterns or inventing props.
The CLI includes a built-in agent docs system that generates context files for your AI tool of choice. One command sets up everything your AI needs to write correct component code.
base._title: Guides › Working with AI › Overview

base.name: quick-start
base.description: Tell your AI to install the CLI and set itself up:
prose: Set up agent docs
Tell your AI to install the CLI and set itself up:
Paste this into your AI Install @astryxdesign/cli and run `astryx init --features agents` to set up your Astryx context. Read the generated file.

That's it. The `init --features agents` command generates everything your AI needs (component index, behavioral rules, CLI reference, and package guidance from configured integrations) from the installed project. After a dependency bump, `astryx upgrade --from <old version>` reports a stale block and adding `--apply` refreshes it.

By default this writes the instructions to `AGENTS.md` (the tool-agnostic standard most agents read), in the project root: the nearest folder whose `package.json` declares an Astryx package, else the nearest with any `package.json`. The search stops at the repository root. In the home folder, or in a settings folder in it outside a project, init writes no agent docs: every folder of the home folder whose name starts with a dot (`~/.claude`, `~/.gemini`, `~/.codex`) is a settings folder, and such a folder itself never counts as a project, even with a `package.json`; a project below it with its own `package.json`, such as an agent worktree, is set up normally. Claude Code skips `AGENTS.md` when the project has a `CLAUDE.md` or `.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so init also writes them to that file, even when it imports `AGENTS.md`: Claude Code does not follow that import in a session started in a subfolder. When both files exist, root `CLAUDE.md` gets the copy and a copy in `.claude/CLAUDE.md` is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`, in which case a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits keeps a copy. Gemini CLI reads only `GEMINI.md`, so init adds a one-line import of `AGENTS.md` there, unless `GEMINI.md` already imports it. `upgrade` keeps the copies in sync. The block between the Astryx markers belongs to Astryx: init and `upgrade` write, refresh, and remove it whatever the project's ignore rules or generated markers say, and never change the text around it. To target a specific tool's file instead:

Manual options astryx init --features agents --agent claude    # CLAUDE.md if present, else .claude/CLAUDE.md
astryx init --features agents --agent cursor    # .cursorrules if present, else AGENTS.md
astryx init --features agents --agent codex     # AGENTS.md (Copilot, Codex, etc.)
astryx init --features agents --agent hermes    # .hermes.md or HERMES.md if present, else AGENTS.md
astryx init --features agents --agent muse      # AGENTS.md (Muse)
astryx init --features agents --agent all       # every agent file present except GEMINI.md, else AGENTS.md and .claude/CLAUDE.md

With `--agent all`, `GEMINI.md` keeps its one-line import of `AGENTS.md`. With `--agent claude` or `--agent all`, as by default, when `CLAUDE.md` gets the instructions, `.claude/CLAUDE.md` gets none and a copy already there is removed, unless the project ignores `CLAUDE.md`: a fresh clone does not have it, so a `.claude/CLAUDE.md` the project commits gets a copy too, with `--agent claude` and `--agent all` alike. `init --remove-agents` removes them at the project root and in the folder it runs in.

For agents that work outside any one project, your global install keeps one short Astryx skill, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, linked into the skill folders agent tools read, such as `~/.claude/skills/astryx`. It tells agents Astryx is there and when to use it; `astryx init --user` writes it now or, with `--remove-agents`, turns it off. Inside a project, agents follow that project's own agent docs. See `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
base._title: Guides › Working with AI › Set up agent docs

base.name: what-gets-generated
base.description: The generated context teaches your AI a 3-step workflow before writing any UI code:
prose: What Gets Generated
The generated context teaches your AI a 3-step workflow before writing any UI code:
`astryx build "<idea>"`: get the page template to start from (always one: the closest match, or the app shell), two other templates, and the blocks and components for the parts it lacks
`astryx template <name> <path>`: scaffold that template into the project, keep its frame and spacing, and replace its content
`astryx component <Name>`: read props and examples for every component used

It also includes rules that prevent common mistakes (start every page from a template, no raw divs, no style={{}}, use tokens not magic values), a CLI quick reference, and package-labeled integration guidance when a configured manifest declares `agentDocs`. After setup, you shouldn't need to manually correct your AI on these conventions; the agent docs handle it at the system level.

base.name: the-astryx-pattern
base.description: AI agents frequently invoke the CLI with incorrect paths (e.g. node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/bin/docs.mjs instead of astryx.mjs), leading to silent failures. Adding an npm script alias with the correct path eliminates this entirely.
prose: The astryx Pattern

AI agents frequently invoke the CLI with incorrect paths (e.g. node_modules/@astryxdesign/cli/bin/docs.mjs instead of astryx.mjs), leading to silent failures. Adding an npm script alias with the correct path eliminates this entirely.
With this alias, agents run `npm run astryx -- component --list` instead of guessing the binary path. The `--` separator is standard npm convention for passing flags to scripts.

Reliable CLI invocation npm run astryx -- component --list
npm run astryx -- component Dialog --dense
npm run astryx -- docs styling --full --detail brief
npm run astryx -- docs tokens --dense

base.name: mcp-server
base.description: Astryx ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that any MCP-compatible AI tool can connect to. Instead of manually pasting CLI output, the AI can query the Astryx design system directly, searching for components, reading full…
prose: MCP Server

Astryx ships a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that any MCP-compatible AI tool can connect to. Instead of manually pasting CLI output, the AI can query the Astryx design system directly, searching for components, reading full documentation, and pulling code examples on demand.
The MCP server exposes two tools: search(query) for discovering components, doc topics, and templates; and get(name) for retrieving full documentation with props, usage, and examples.

Add the server to your MCP config file. The entry is a remote HTTP server, and the exact shape differs per client, so use the snippet for the tool you run. An entry with an unrecognized transport is skipped with a warning rather than an error, which reads as a server that connects but exposes no tools.
Claude Code can also write that entry from the terminal:
claude mcp add --transport http astryx https://astryx.atmeta.com/mcp
Claude Desktop is the exception: claude_desktop_config.json holds local stdio servers, so a remote server is added through Settings, then Connectors, then Add custom connector, pasting the URL above.

Once connected, your AI tool can search for components by natural language (e.g. "dropdown menu", "success message") and retrieve full documentation without any manual CLI invocation. The server uses the same keyword index from component docs, so search quality improves automatically as component documentation is updated.

base.name: authoring
base.description: Build an npm package that adds components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods to Astryx apps, and look up every field of every file it holds.
prose: Authoring

In global mode: users can install your integration for their computer, beside the global CLI. It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

An integration is a way to share things with Astryx users: a package you own and maintain, built on a framework Astryx gives you. Publish one, many, or any mix, and people install it in one step. It works with the Astryx CLI alongside Core. See each kind under `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks`.
For example, ship a carousel as an integration. Any app that installs it can find it with `astryx search carousel`, and the CLI uses it like any Astryx Core component.
An integration can also replace a built-in template or doc. To start, install `@astryxdesign/cli` and open `astryx docs authoring/quick-start`.
Every field of every file you write for an integration is in `astryx docs authoring/field-reference`.

Every integration runs `astryx integration check --strict` in its own build: it is required, not optional, so a doc, prop, or link that stops matching the code fails your build instead of your users' apps. See `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
base._title: Authoring

base.name: building-blocks
base.description: Add components, templates, themes, docs, and codemods, and configure how it behaves.
prose: Building Blocks

In global mode: every kind your package adds also applies outside projects when users install it for their computer, beside the global CLI; inside a project, only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
These are everything you can add to an integration. Mix them however you like. You are not limited to any one thing.
One component, or a whole library of them.
Components together with themes and templates.
Only docs, if that is all you need.
Agent guidance, so the AI agents in an app follow your library.
Codemods that update app code across your breaking changes.
Each kind below is its own guide. Open one to learn, in depth, how to add it and how to keep it healthy as your package grows.

base.name: add-a-codemod
base.description: `integration add codemod` writes a codemod into a folder named after a version. Apps run it with `astryx upgrade` to migrate their code.
prose: Add a codemod
`integration add codemod` writes a codemod into a folder named after a version. Apps run it with `astryx upgrade` to migrate their code.
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0

codemods/
  0.7.0/
    rename-delay.mjs         # the codemod
    rename-delay.test.mjs    # skipped: a test file
    __tests__/               # skipped: a test folder

The first add declares `codemods: './codemods'` in `astryx.integration.mjs`. The codemod's id is its path inside the version folder, without the extension: `rename-delay`. An id must be unique across all version folders in the package.

The loader skips `*.test.*`, `*.spec.*`, and `*.fixture.*` files and everything under `__tests__/` or `__fixtures__/`, so tests can sit beside the codemod. The folder name decides when an app runs the codemod; see "Choose when a codemod runs".

base.name: write-the-transform
base.description: A codemod default-exports a plain object with a `type`, a `title`, and a `transform` function. `transform` returns the new source, or `null` to leave the file as it is.
prose: Write the transform
A codemod default-exports a plain object with a `type`, a `title`, and a `transform` function. `transform` returns the new source, or `null` to leave the file as it is.

`type: 'code'` rewrites the app's source files that match `fileExtensions`. `type: 'config'` rewrites the app's `astryx.config` file instead, and runs before code codemods. `title` shows in the upgrade output, and `api.jscodeshift` is a jscodeshift instance for the file. Every field is in `astryx docs authoring codemod`.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Codemods › Write the transform

base.name: which-codemods-run
base.description: Two rules decide whether an app's `astryx upgrade` runs your codemods: the app's Core versions, and whether the app names your package.
prose: Choose when a codemod runs
Two rules decide whether an app's `astryx upgrade` runs your codemods: the app's Core versions, and whether the app names your package.

Version folders are matched against the app's `@astryxdesign/core` versions, not your package's version. `upgrade --from <version>` runs each folder above `--from`, up to and including the Core version installed in the app. With Core 0.7.0 installed, `--from 0.6.3` runs `0.7.0/`, and `--from 0.7.0` runs nothing. A folder named after your own release, such as `1.0.0/`, waits until the app has Core 1.0.0.

`upgrade` runs your codemods only when the app lists your package in `integrations` in its `astryx.config`, or passes `--integration @acme/astryx-widgets`. Having your package installed is not enough: the run then skips your codemods with no warning.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Codemods › Choose when a codemod runs

base.name: run-codemods-in-an-app
base.description: An app previews codemods with `astryx upgrade` and writes the changes with `--apply`. Without `--apply`, nothing on disk changes.
prose: Run codemods in an app
An app previews codemods with `astryx upgrade` and writes the changes with `--apply`. Without `--apply`, nothing on disk changes.

# Preview each codemod and the files it would change
astryx upgrade --from 0.6.3 --integration @acme/astryx-widgets
# Write the changes
astryx upgrade --from 0.6.3 --integration @acme/astryx-widgets --apply

Integrations: @acme/astryx-widgets
<n> codemods to run (dry run)
Applying integration codemods...
  Rename AcmeCarousel delay to interval (v0.7.0, @acme/astryx-widgets)
!     ~ src/Hero.tsx (would change)
`<n>` counts Core's codemods for the same versions too: they run first and print above `Integrations:`. To run only yours, as when you test it, add `--codemod rename-delay`.

`--from` is the Core version the app had before it upgraded. The run scans `./src` unless the app passes `--path`, and it never writes a file the app marks as generated, vendored, or ignored; see `astryx docs cli/commands/upgrade`. `upgrade --list` shows only Core codemods.
An integration manifest has no `hooks` field. Commands that run after codemods, such as a formatter, are the app's to set, in `hooks.postCodemod` in its `astryx.config`.

base.name: export-the-component
base.description: Apps copy the component doc's `import` field into their code, so that exact specifier must resolve from your packed package. `integration add` writes it together with an `exports` entry in package.json.
prose: Export the component

Apps copy the component doc's `import` field into their code, so that exact specifier must resolve from your packed package. `integration add` writes it together with an `exports` entry in package.json.
Add writes the entry only when package.json already has an `exports` map, so start every package with `"exports": {}`.

A file does not have to be named after its component. When `Slides.tsx` exports `AcmeCarousel` and nothing named `Slides`, keep the doc beside it as `Slides.doc.mjs` and set its `name` to `AcmeCarousel`: apps list, search and open the component by that name, and `integration verify` checks that its import exports `AcmeCarousel`. A file that exports its own name keeps that name. A package that names its files in kebab case works the same way: `acme-gallery.doc.mjs` beside `acme-gallery.tsx` sets `name: 'AcmeGallery'`.

The file name still opens the doc. A name that Core or another doc's file already has stays theirs, and so does a Core name your package replaces: with `Badge.doc.mjs` naming `AcmeBadge`, `astryx component Badge` opens Core's `Badge`, and `--package` with your package name reaches yours.

base.description: `integration verify` unpacks the packed package into a temporary app, resolves each documented import, and checks that the module exports the documented component name. Its `--json` output names each failure by code.
prose: Verify the packed import

`integration verify` unpacks the packed package into a temporary app, resolves each documented import, and checks that the module exports the documented component name. Its `--json` output names each failure by code.
astryx integration verify
`component_import_unresolvable` means the exports map has no entry for the documented import.
`component_export_missing` means the module does not export the documented name, or package.json has no exports map.
`typescript_extension_in_specifier` means the public import ends in `.ts` or `.tsx`.
To import from the package root, set `import: '@acme/astryx-widgets'` and re-export the component from the file that `exports["."]` points to. See `astryx docs cli/commands/integration-verify`.

base.description: Write and maintain the default component doc, then adapt it when one family owns several exports or a member needs its own file.
prose: Describe the component

A component's `.doc.mjs` is part of the integration's public contract, not optional commentary. Astryx uses it for CLI output and search, and people and agents read it to decide whether the component fits and how to use it.
Change the source and its `.doc.mjs` together.
Update the doc whenever the public name, import, behavior, props, defaults, examples, or accessibility requirements change.

`integration verify` checks the doc shape and packed import, and `doctor integration components` compares each props table with the component's TypeScript props (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components/describe-the-component/check-the-props`). Neither can prove the prose still matches the component.
Every component doc has one stable identity and enough usage guidance for a reader to choose it correctly. Pick the shape below that matches your module.
After every source or doc change, read the component back. This output is what people and agents receive.
astryx component AcmeCarousel

prose: Run the props check

`doctor integration components` compares every props table in your component docs, hidden docs and every family entry included, with the props the component's TypeScript declares. Run it in your package after you change a component or its doc.
astryx doctor integration components

severity:  [warn]
component: AcmeCarousel
prop:      loop
kind:      not_in_code
message:   "loop" is documented, but AcmeCarousel's props have no "loop".
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
source:    components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
docType:   boolean

1 prop(s) differ between the docs and the code in 1 of 1 component(s) compared (TypeScript 6.0.3). These are warnings: update the doc, or the code if the doc is right.
A doc's own `props` describe the export its `name` names. In a family doc, each entry describes its own export. A hook entry documents parameters and returns, so it is not compared.

It reads props with the `typescript` your package installs, and reads your package's `tsconfig.json` the way `tsc -p` does. It finds TypeScript the way the docs check does, TypeScript 7 included (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/check-your-docs`). Without a usable one it prints `[skip] Props not compared` and the reason.
Findings are warnings and leave the exit code at 0. Read them before you publish. With `--json`, they are in `data.propDrift.findings`.

base.name: fix-each-finding
base.description: Each finding's `kind` says what differs. Fix the doc, or the code if the doc is right.
prose: Fix each finding
Each finding's `kind` says what differs. Fix the doc, or the code if the doc is right.
not_in_code The doc lists a prop the component's props do not have Remove it from the doc, or add it to the code. A name an index signature takes, such as data-*, counts as present

not_in_doc Your package declares a prop the doc does not list, or builds one with a mapped type, such as Partial<Record<'sm' | 'md', string>> Document it. Props from React, the DOM, or another package are never asked for, and neither are props whose keys another package defines (keyof CSSProperties, behind an alias or not), className, style, xstyle, data-testid, ref, key, or a prop whose JSDoc has @internal. A deprecated prop is still a prop: document it until you remove it. A prop a mapped type builds from keys the check cannot trace (a template literal, say) is listed under [info] Props not checked for a doc entry instead

required_mismatch required disagrees with the code Set required: true exactly when every caller must pass the prop. One your defaultProps fills counts as optional, as it is to JSX callers, and so does one only some members of a union require, since a caller can leave it out: say in its description which variants need it. An entry that names several props (value / onChange) makes the same claim about each: give them separate entries when they differ
type_mismatch The documented type differs from the code's, where both read exactly Copy the type from the source, or fix the code. The next section says which types are judged

default_mismatch The documented default differs from the literal default the component writes in its props destructuring, such as size = 'md' Copy the default from the source, quoted as code: default: "'md'". Quotes and spacing are ignored, and a default that is not a literal on either side (a constant, a call, prose) is not compared

base.name: write-types-the-check-can-judge
keywords: Write types the check can judge
base.description: For a prop your package declares, the check also compares the documented `type`, but only where both sides read exactly. It never guesses, so a type it cannot judge is listed, not reported. It needs TypeScript 4.8 or later: with an older…
prose: Write types the check can judge

For a prop your package declares, the check also compares the documented `type`, but only where both sides read exactly. It never guesses, so a type it cannot judge is listed, not reported. It needs TypeScript 4.8 or later: with an older one it prints `[skip] Prop types not judged` and judges none.

severity:  [warn]
component: AcmeCarousel
prop:      interval
kind:      type_mismatch
message:   "interval" is documented as string, but the code declares number.
doc:       components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
source:    components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
docType:   string
codeType:  number

Write the type as the source writes it, such as `ReactNode[]` or `(index: number) => void`. Parameter names, member order, quotes and whitespace may differ. Text that writes `readonly` must match exactly, parameter names included; only whitespace may differ. `React.X` names React's own `X` where the prop is declared, so it matches a bare `X` only where that name is React's: `React.KeyboardEvent` is not the DOM's `KeyboardEvent`.

Name a type as the file that declares the prop names it, so an import renamed there (`Item as BaseItem`) is written as that file writes it. A field (`cfg.level`) takes its prop's file, even when the field's own type is declared in another file.

A type written another way is judged only when both sides are built from exact parts: primitives such as `string` and `number`, string, number and boolean literals, string enum members, arrays and unions of these, and type names that stand for them. Union members may come in any order, and a member another covers adds nothing, as TypeScript passes it there: `undefined` beside `void`, or `string[]` beside `(string | number)[]`.
A mutable array type matches a readonly one, because callers can pass it. A readonly one documented for a mutable array is a mismatch.

When a prop's variants give a field different types, as `{value: string} | {value: number}` does, document every variant's type (`string | number`). The types of only some variants are listed: the prop's variants give this field different types. With more than six variant types, any other type is listed too.
To name an alias and show its values, write `AcmeSize = 'sm' | 'md'` or `AcmeSize ('sm' | 'md')`. Both parts must match.
An optional prop's `undefined` is set aside on both sides. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, the doc shows `undefined` exactly when the code declares it.
Anything else, such as an object, a tuple, a generic with arguments, `keyof`, an intersection, or a mapped or conditional type written another way, is not compared.

The check prints how many documented types it judged, then lists the rest by reason: not a form the check judges exactly, a field the prop's variants give different types, a standard prop, or a prop declared outside the package. With `--json`, they are in `data.propDrift.typesNotCompared`.

[info] Documented prop types judged: 2; not compared: 0. A type is judged when the doc writes it the same as the source (exactly, if it contains `readonly`), or when both are primitives, literals, arrays and unions of those, or names for them.
titles: Write types the check can judge

Put the primary or most-used export first.
Use a full entry when this file owns that export's description and signature.
Use `props` for a component entry. Use `params` and `returns` for a hook entry.
Do not add private implementation helpers or exports that people should not use directly.

base.name: document-the-family-inline
base.description: The public module named by `import` must export every component or hook named by a full entry. Apps then list, search and open each component in the family by its own name. A full entry the module does not export is not listed, and…
prose: Document the family inline

The public module named by `import` must export every component or hook named by a full entry. Apps then list, search and open each component in the family by its own name. A full entry the module does not export is not listed, and `integration verify` does not report it: check the family with `astryx component --list`. When `import` names output your pack lifecycle builds (such as `dist`), the members are listed once that output exists, and `integration verify` compares them as they are listed after the pack builds it.

A member's source is the `.tsx` file in the family doc's folder, or below it, that declares it: the one the family's own file or the module `import` names reaches, else the one in that folder that declares the name, as when `import` names built output. A member that only a bundle or a file outside that folder declares is still listed, with no source for `--source` or `swizzle`. A member is not listed when a doc's file or a Core name your package replaces already has its name. A member that shares a name with Core opens with `--package`.

base.name: decide-whether-to-replace
base.description: Most components should not use `replaces`. Give a new component its own name and let apps choose it explicitly. Replace Core only when your component must become the default for one Core identity everywhere the integration is active.
prose: Decide whether to replace

Most components should not use `replaces`. Give a new component its own name and let apps choose it explicitly. Replace Core only when your component must become the default for one Core identity everywhere the integration is active.
Use it when
Your component intentionally serves the same role as one specific Core component.
Every app that loads the integration should get your component from unqualified component detail, `component --list`, search, `swizzle <Name>`, and issue routing.
You have tested both the replacement and explicit access to the original Core component.
Do not use it when
Your component is an alternative, variant, wrapper, or product-specific extension. Give it a unique name instead.
You only need to resolve an accidental name collision.
You want the replacement in only one screen or workflow. Replacement applies across the app wherever the integration is active.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Components › Replace a Core component › Decide whether to replace

base.name: set-the-replacement
base.description: Every field is in `astryx docs authoring component-doc`.
prose: Set the replacement
Every field is in `astryx docs authoring component-doc`.
The replacement turns on only when your package declares the first CLI release that applies it. Add this to its `package.json`:

Any `@astryxdesign/cli` range that starts at that release or later turns it on, including the `>=0.7.0` that `integration add doc --parent` wrote in published 0.6.4 and 0.6.5, and `integration add theme` in published 0.6.5.

Without such a range, the component keeps its own name, the Core component stays selected (a component named like its target stays ambiguous by that bare name, as before), and `doctor integration components` warns with the range to add. Apps that load such a package see no change.
`replaces` names the Core `ComponentDoc` identity, not its display label, import path, or a standalone hook.
Your component may keep a distinct name or use the same name as the target. A distinct name remains directly addressable on older CLIs that ignore `replaces`.
`--package @astryxdesign/core` always selects the original Core component, and `--package` with your package selects your component by either name.
Replacing `SideNav` replaces only that name. `SideNavItem` and the other SideNav parts stay Core components; document any parts your package provides under their own names.
`swizzle --list` lists Core components, including the one you replace. `swizzle SideNav` copies your component, and `swizzle SideNav --package @astryxdesign/core` copies the original.

base.name: check-replacement-resolution
base.description: Once the package declares the range, a missing target, invalid value, second replacement for one target in the same package, or a replacement named after a different Core component is an error. Without the range, `doctor integration…
prose: Check replacement resolution

astryx doctor integration components
astryx component SideNav
astryx component AcmeSideNav
astryx component SideNav --package @astryxdesign/core

Once the package declares the range, a missing target, invalid value, second replacement for one target in the same package, or a replacement named after a different Core component is an error. Without the range, `doctor integration components` reports each of these as a warning.

When several integrations replace one target, explicit configuration beats the automatic pick. Among explicitly configured integrations, the later package wins and Doctor warns. Among autolinked integrations alone, the dependency listed later in `package.json` wins and Doctor warns.

base.name: keep-within-the-limits
base.description: Every line costs space in each app's agent file, so the CLI keeps guidance short and few. Put detail in your docs instead.
prose: Keep within the limits
Every line costs space in each app's agent file, so the CLI keeps guidance short and few. Put detail in your docs instead.
8 lines per package integration add fails: append may contain at most 8 lines.
240 characters per line integration add fails: must contain at most 240 Unicode code points.
32 lines per app, from all its packages init writes no agent block and prints Could not install agent docs.
A line is one line of plain text. Line breaks, control characters, spaces at either end, and managed-block markers such as `<!-- ASTRYX:START -->` are rejected.

Start a command in a line with the word astryx alone, with no runner in front, as in: Run astryx doctor before finishing. The block names the command the app runs once, at its top, for every command below it, so your line works in every app. See `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/configuration/cli-command`.

base.name: when-to-set-it
base.description: The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as…
prose: When to set it

The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`, when the app's own CLI answered, and otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `npx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2`.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI some other way, such as a wrapper your company ships that runs it with your package loaded. Otherwise the commands the CLI prints send them, and their agents, to a CLI that answers without your package. Most packages leave it out.

If two packages an app loads set different commands, the CLI uses neither: it prints commands with what the app's package manager runs, even when a host tool named a command. `astryx doctor` warns in its `cli-command` check and names both packages:

label:   CLI command
message: Loaded integrations declare different CLI commands: @acme/astryx-widgets (`acme astryx`), @other/kit (`other astryx`). Neither is used, so printed commands start with `pnpm exec astryx`.

base.name: record-runs-with-debug
base.description: Export a `debug` function from `astryx.integration.mjs`; the CLI calls it once per command run in an app loading your package.
prose: Record runs with debug
Export a `debug` function from `astryx.integration.mjs`; the CLI calls it once per command run in an app loading your package.
The event is a `DebugEvent` with `command`, `outcome`, `exitCode`, `durationMs`, `error`, and more, its values scrubbed (`redacted: true`). Every field is in `astryx docs authoring debug-event`.

Keep the function synchronous: the CLI calls it as the process exits and never waits for a promise. The app's own `debug` handler runs first, then yours. A handler that throws is skipped, and the command's output and exit code stay the same.

An app records every command only when its `astryx.config` names `integrations` or `debug`, as listing your package does. Otherwise your handler runs only for commands loading the app's project, such as `component` and `docs`, never for `--version` or a mistyped command. In an app whose config names neither word, those commands also print a stderr warning.
`debug` is a named export, not a manifest field, so an older CLI ignores it and loads the rest of your manifest.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Configuration › Debug and gap reports › Record runs with debug

prose: Turn off debug in an app
An app can refuse every integration's `debug` handler and keep its own. It sets `inheritDebug` in its package.json:
{"astryx": {"inheritDebug": false}}
Your handler then no longer runs in that app.

base.name: handle-gap-reports
base.description: Export a `gapReport` handler, and `astryx gap-report` in an app sends it each gap report, such as a missing component or variant. The handler files the report and returns a receipt.
prose: Handle gap reports
Export a `gapReport` handler, and `astryx gap-report` in an app sends it each gap report, such as a missing component or variant. The handler files the report and returns a receipt.
Every handler in the app gets every report, so check `report.target.package` and skip reports about other packages.
Every field is in `astryx docs authoring gap-report-handler`.

The CLI waits 30 seconds, then aborts `signal`. A throw, a timeout, or an invalid receipt fails your delivery, and the command exits 1; the other handlers still run. Like `debug`, `gapReport` is a named export that older CLIs ignore.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Configuration › Debug and gap reports › Handle gap reports

base.name: ask-before-filing-in-public
base.description: Set `audience: 'public'` when your handler writes somewhere the public can read. The CLI runs it only when the caller passes `--confirm-public`; an `'internal'` handler always runs.
prose: Ask before filing in public
Set `audience: 'public'` when your handler writes somewhere the public can read. The CLI runs it only when the caller passes `--confirm-public`; an `'internal'` handler always runs.
astryx gap-report AcmeCarousel --category missing_variant --reason 'Need a vertical layout'

handlerType: integration
handler:     @acme/astryx-widgets
audience:    public
status:      consent_required
message:     Rerun with --confirm-public to file this report.
With `--confirm-public`, the same delivery reads `status: filed` and shows your `url`. The report goes to the package named by `--package`, else the package that owns the component, else Core.

prose: Fall back to issuesUrl
With no `gapReport` handler in the app, the CLI routes the report to the target package's manifest `issuesUrl`.
A GitHub issues URL, such as `https://github.com/acme/widgets/issues`, gets an issue filed with the GitHub CLI, `gh`, once the caller passes `--confirm-public`.
Any other URL comes back as a `routed_only` receipt for the caller to open.
With no `issuesUrl`, the command fails: `Package "@acme/astryx-widgets" provides neither a report handler nor an issues URL.`

One handler anywhere in the app, from the app or from any package, turns the fallback off for every report. So does a listed package that fails to load: the CLI cannot tell whether it has a handler, so the report fails for that package instead of going to another tracker. See `astryx docs cli/commands/gap-report`.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Configuration › Debug and gap reports › Fall back to issuesUrl

base.name: choose-a-destination
keywords: Let the person choose where a report goes
base.description: When an app loads packages naming their own `issuesUrl`, a report can go to the default (the handlers, or the fallback above) or to one of those packages. `astryx gap-report --list-categories` and the receipt of a report filed without…
prose: Let the person choose where a report goes

When an app loads packages naming their own `issuesUrl`, a report can go to the default (the handlers, or the fallback above) or to one of those packages. `astryx gap-report --list-categories` and the receipt of a report filed without `--to` list every destination, with a line telling the agent to ask the person.
An agent asks the person where to file. It never picks a package destination on its own.
`--to <package>` carries the person's choice: the report goes only to that package's `issuesUrl`, under the same `--confirm-public` rule, and no handler runs.
Without a choice, leave out `--to`; the report goes to the default.
A `--to` that names no destination fails before anything is sent and lists the destinations.

keywords: Add a topic with the CLI
base.description: Run `integration add doc` in your package to add a topic. It writes the topic file and declares the `docs` root in `astryx.integration.mjs`.
prose: Add a topic with the CLI
Run `integration add doc` in your package to add a topic. It writes the topic file and declares the `docs` root in `astryx.integration.mjs`.

astryx integration add doc deploying
# Read it the way an app will
astryx docs deploying

doc contribution added

[ok] deploying

Declare doc root ./docs in astryx.integration.mjs.

- docs/deploying.doc.mjs
- astryx.integration.mjs
Name the topic in lowercase kebab-case, such as `deploying`. Readers type the name as a command argument, so it holds only letters, digits, `_`, and `-`.
Keep the name stable: readers and links find the topic by it.

Pick a name `astryx docs` does not already list: no Core topic, and no section such as `tokens` or `layout`. To take over or add to a Core topic, see `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/extend-or-replace`.

base.description: A topic is a plain object with `type: 'generic'`, a `name`, a `title`, a one-sentence `description`, and `sections`. Each section has a `title` and a list of `content` blocks.
prose: Write the sections
A topic is a plain object with `type: 'generic'`, a `name`, a `title`, a one-sentence `description`, and `sections`. Each section has a `title` and a list of `content` blocks.

The sample sets a section `id`, so `package.json` needs the CLI peer `"@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.4"`. Published 0.6.3 and earlier reject `id` and hide every doc topic your package ships, and `integration verify` fails without that peer; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`.

Every field is in `astryx docs authoring reference-doc`.

base.name: write-commands-without-a-runner
base.description: Write an Astryx command as `{@command doctor}` and a package-manager step as `{@pm install @acme/widgets}`, never with a runner such as npx or pnpm exec, or a package manager's own command, in front. The CLI shows each one with the…
prose: Write commands for every reader

Write an Astryx command as `{@command doctor}` and a package-manager step as `{@pm install @acme/widgets}`, never with a runner such as npx or pnpm exec, or a package manager's own command, in front. The CLI shows each one with the command the reader runs: `pnpm exec astryx doctor` or `yarn astryx doctor`, `pnpm add @acme/widgets` or `npm install @acme/widgets`, or the `cliCommand` an integration sets. `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/doc-syntax` lists every token. A command written bare, the word astryx and a command, is shown the same way. `doctor integration validate` (and so `integration check`) names each command written another way, with the token that replaces it; `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/doc-syntax` lists what it checks. An install step, which runs before the CLI is installed, is `{@pm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init}`.

docs/deploying.doc.mjs {type: 'prose', text: 'Check the app with {@command doctor} before you ship.'},
{type: 'code', lang: 'bash', code: '{@command doctor}'},

Read in an app whose integration sets cliCommand: 'acme astryx' Check the app with `acme astryx doctor` before you ship.

```bash
acme astryx doctor
```

The CLI prefixes an inline code span that starts with the word astryx, a command at the start of a line, or after `&&`, `||`, `;` or `|`, in a `bash`, `sh`, `shell`, `zsh`, `console`, `text` or `markdown` code block or one with no language, and a table cell that holds only a command.
Code in other languages, such as a `js` example, and the word astryx in plain prose stay as written.
`--json` returns the doc as written, so a reader that shows it prefixes the commands itself.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Add a topic › Write commands for every reader

base.description: Every doc is a `.doc.mjs` file whose `type` says what it describes. `integration add` writes the right `type` and file for each kind.
prose: Pick the doc kind
Every doc is a `.doc.mjs` file whose `type` says what it describes. `integration add` writes the right `type` and file for each kind.
A guide or topic 'generic' docs/deploying.doc.mjs
Your package's docs section 'namespace' docs/acme.doc.mjs
A component 'component' components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs, beside AcmeCarousel.tsx
A template 'page' or 'block' templates/acme-dashboard.doc.mjs, beside acme-dashboard.tsx
A theme 'theme' themes/ocean/oceanTheme.doc.mjs, beside oceanTheme.ts

Only guides, topics, and your docs section go in the `docs` root. The others have their own guides: `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components`, `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates`, and `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/themes`.

prose: Keep topics in the docs root
The `docs` field in `astryx.integration.mjs` names the folder that holds your topics. The CLI reads every `.doc.mjs` file under it, in subfolders too.
Readers open a topic by its `name`, not its file name. Name the file after the doc, `<name>.doc.mjs`, so each one is easy to find.
A topic with no `placement` is a flat topic: the docs list shows it under Topics, and readers open it by its name.
For a section of your own in the docs tree, see `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/sections-and-placement`.

base.name: run-the-docs-check
base.description: Run `doctor integration docs` in your package to check the docs tree, every link, and overlaps with Core topics, and to list any passage two topics repeat. Pass a package name to check an installed package.
prose: Run the docs check

Run `doctor integration docs` in your package to check the docs tree, every link, and overlaps with Core topics, and to list any passage two topics repeat. Pass a package name to check an installed package.

astryx doctor integration docs
# In an app, check an installed package
astryx doctor integration docs @acme/astryx-widgets

Checking integration docs: @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

[ok] The docs tree and every link in these docs check out.

[ok] No doc topics overlap with Core.
[ok] No topic copies a passage from another.
[ok] No filler phrases or low-density topics.

Write each fact in one topic. When two of your topics, or one of yours and a Core topic, repeat 10 or more words of prose word for word, the check lists the pair as a `copied_passage` warning. It names the topic that keeps the text (a Core topic, or of your two the one the passage fits) and the line in the other where to put the link instead (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/links`). Code and examples are not compared, and a topic may carry the text of the Core topic it replaces. A run with fewer than 4 distinct content words (words other than function words such as "the", "in" or "it"), or one that three or more topics share (a series lead-in), is not listed. Each listed pair is also a warning (`copied_passage`): `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you fix it.

Keep docs dense. The check lists, as a `doc_fluff` warning, each padding phrase in your prose, with its file line and what to write instead, and each topic of 80 or more prose words in which fewer than half the words carry content (words other than function words such as the, and, in), with its measured share and the floor of 0.5. `doctor integration docs` still exits 0, and `integration check --strict` fails until you cut it. Code, examples, and quoted text are not read. The phrases: `it's important to note`, `it is important to note`, `important to note that`, `it's worth noting`, `it is worth noting`, `worth noting that`, `it should be noted`, `please note`, `note that` (opening a sentence), `as mentioned above`, `as mentioned earlier`, `as mentioned before`, `as noted above`, `as you can see`, `needless to say`, `in order to`, `due to the fact that`, `for the purpose of`, `at this point in time`, `in other words`, `basically`, `essentially`, `obviously`.

Point at another doc with a link, never by writing `astryx docs <name>` in prose: `{@link generic:<name>}` for one of your package's topics, or `{@link @astryxdesign/cli:generic:<name>}` for a Core doc (`namespace:` for a Core namespace). The CLI prints the link as the command that opens the doc, and doctor checks that the doc exists. The check lists each written pointer to a doc that exists as a `stray_doc_pointer` warning, with the link to write instead. A command with more words, or one in a code block, is a walkthrough and is not listed.
Its arguments and exit codes are in `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor-integration-docs`.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Check your docs › Run the docs check

base.name: know-what-fails-the-check
base.description: A doc that does not load, an accidental Core overlap, a `reference` block that names no doc, or a failed namespace or placement fails the check with exit code 1. A link that names no doc only warns, and the exit code stays 0.
prose: Know what fails the check

A doc that does not load, an accidental Core overlap, a `reference` block that names no doc, or a failed namespace or placement fails the check with exit code 1. A link that names no doc only warns, and the exit code stays 0.
A doc that does not load, such as an unknown section field or block type [fail] invalid_doc 1
A topic with a Core topic's name and no replaces or extends [fail] accidental 1
A placement that fails, which hides the doc [fail] invalid_doc_graph 1
A reference block whose target names no doc [fail] invalid_doc_reference 1
A link that names no doc [warn] invalid_doc_graph 0
A topic that sets replaces or extends [info] replaces or extends 0
Read the warnings before you publish. With `--json`, they are in `data.issues`, with `severity: "warning"`.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Check your docs › Know what fails the check

base.name: check-each-doc-against-its-type
keywords: Check each doc against its type
base.description: `doctor integration validate` reads every doc your package ships against the type `@astryxdesign/cli/authoring` publishes for its kind, the way `tsc` would: a `hidden` doc and a second doc for one name too. Test fixtures under `__tests__`…
prose: Check each doc against its type

`doctor integration validate` reads every doc your package ships against the type `@astryxdesign/cli/authoring` publishes for its kind, the way `tsc` would: a `hidden` doc and a second doc for one name too. Test fixtures under `__tests__` in the components or docs root, which those readers skip, are counted, not checked. It reports a field the type does not have (`unknown_field`), a missing required field (`missing_field`), and a value outside the field's type (`wrong_type`).
astryx doctor integration validate

Checking 1 doc(s) against the authoring types (TypeScript 6.0.3)

severity: [warn]
doc:      components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
line:     7
export:   default
type:     ComponentDoc
field:    summary
problem:  unknown_field
message:  Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'summary' does not exist in type 'SingleComponentDoc'.
fix:      Remove `summary`: SingleComponentDoc has no field `summary`.

The folder decides the type: `ComponentDoc` in your components root, `IntegrationTemplateDoc` in your templates root, `ThemeDoc` in your themes root, and in your docs root the type the doc's `type` names. Keep the `@type` comment above each doc's export too, so your editor shows the same problems as you type.
Every finding is a warning, so the exit code stays 0. With `--json`, they are in `data.docTypes.findings`.

It uses the `typescript` your package installs. Where `typescript` is missing or has no JavaScript compiler API, as TypeScript 7 does, it uses `@typescript/typescript6`, the TypeScript 6 API package, if your package installs it. Without either, it prints `[skip] Docs not type-checked` and the reason.
Every field of every doc type is in `astryx docs authoring/field-reference`.
titles: Check each doc against its type
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Check your docs › Check each doc against its type

base.description: `integration verify` fails a package that ships a docs section, a placed guide, or a doc section with an `id` without an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`. It does not run the docs check, so run both.
prose: Check the CLI peer

`integration verify` fails a package that ships a docs section, a placed guide, or a doc section with an `id` without an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer of `>=0.6.4`. It does not run the docs check, so run both.
astryx integration verify

- [fail] The package ships a namespace doc or a placed guide but declares no @astryxdesign/cli peer. A stable CLI before 0.6.4 does not read the docs tree, and can hide every doc topic the package ships. Declare "@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.4" in peerDependencies (optional in peerDependenciesMeta, if the CLI is not required).
`integration add doc --parent` writes the peer for you.
`integration verify` passes a hidden guide and an accidental Core overlap; only `doctor integration docs` catches them.
Everything else it checks is in `astryx docs cli/commands/integration-verify` and `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.

base.name: the-tokens
base.description: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table…
prose: The tokens

A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.
{@link generic:deploying} another doc the command that opens that doc
astryx docs theme an Astryx command pnpm exec astryx docs theme
npm install -D @acme/widgets a package-manager step pnpm add -D @acme/widgets
npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why) a step only one package manager can do npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why)
{@pm install x} a token shown as written npm install x

In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › The tokens

base.name: package-manager-steps
base.description: A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
prose: Package-manager steps
A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
npm install npm install pnpm install yarn install bun install
npm install x npm install x pnpm add x yarn add x bun add x
npm install -D x npm install -D x pnpm add -D x yarn add -D x bun add -d x
npm install -g x npm install -g x pnpm add -g x yarn global add x (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer bun add -g x
npm uninstall x npm uninstall x pnpm remove x yarn remove x bun remove x
npm install x@latest npm install x@latest pnpm update --latest x yarn up x bun update --latest x
npm run build -- --watch npm run build -- --watch pnpm run build --watch yarn run build --watch bun run build --watch
npx tsc npx tsc pnpm exec tsc yarn run tsc bunx tsc
npx @astryxdesign/cli init npx @astryxdesign/cli init pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init yarn dlx … (npx on Yarn 1) bunx @astryxdesign/cli init
npm create vite npm create vite pnpm create vite yarn create vite bun create vite
Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › Package-manager steps

base.name: one-package-manager
keywords: A step only one package manager can do
base.description: Some commands exist in one package manager only, such as `npm pkg set` or `pnpm setup`. Write `{@pm-only <manager> "<reason>" <command>}`: the manager is one of npm, pnpm, yarn, yarn-classic or bun, and the reason, in double quotes, is…
prose: A step only one package manager can do

Some commands exist in one package manager only, such as `npm pkg set` or `pnpm setup`. Write `{@pm-only <manager> "<reason>" <command>}`: the manager is one of npm, pnpm, yarn, yarn-classic or bun, and the reason, in double quotes, is shown to readers beside the command. Use it only when no `{@pm}` step does the same: doctor names a one-manager step that every package manager can run, with the `{@pm}` token to write.
titles: A step only one package manager can do

base.name: what-doctor-checks
base.description: `doctor integration validate`, and so `integration check`, lists each of these as a note with its file, line and the token to write. A note fails nothing today; the next minor release turns them into warnings, so `integration check…
prose: What doctor checks

`doctor integration validate`, and so `integration check`, lists each of these as a note with its file, line and the token to write. A note fails nothing today; the next minor release turns them into warnings, so `integration check --strict --next` fails on them now. Run it to fix them ahead.
package_manager_command a code span or shell line written for one package manager, such as npm install -D x
runner_command an Astryx command written with a runner, such as pnpm exec astryx docs
plain_command an Astryx command written bare, where astryx docs checks that the command exists
doc_token a token that does not parse, or a name that is not a doc token

In global mode: outside a project, a `{@command}` token prints the way your global install prints every command, and a `{@pm}` step prints for npm unless the CLI detects another package manager. In a project, the project's own runner and package manager decide. See `astryx docs global`.

base.name: replace-a-topic
base.description: Set `replaces` to take over an existing topic, such as Core's `getting-started`. Readers who open the old name get your topic.
prose: Replace a topic
Set `replaces` to take over an existing topic, such as Core's `getting-started`. Readers who open the old name get your topic.

astryx integration add doc acme-getting-started --replaces getting-started
# The old name now opens your topic
astryx docs getting-started

The docs list shows your topic in place of the old one. Because your topic has its own `name`, the old name keeps resolving to it, so links and agents that learned the old name still land on your topic.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Extend or replace a topic › Replace a topic

base.name: extend-a-topic
base.description: Set `extends` to merge sections into an existing topic instead of owning it. A section replaces the base section it matches, and a section that matches none is added at the end.
prose: Extend a topic
Set `extends` to merge sections into an existing topic instead of owning it. A section replaces the base section it matches, and a section that matches none is added at the end.

astryx integration add doc acme-theming --extends theme
astryx docs theme --index

Read the base topic's keys with `--index`, and give a section that replaces one that key as its `id`. A section that replaces one keeps its place. A section without an `id` matches only a base section with exactly its title, or one whose `id` is the key its title makes, so `Integration Themes` is added beside a base `Integration themes` that has no `id`.

Set `before` or `after` to a base section's key to add a new section there instead of at the end. A key that names no section adds it at the end, and `astryx doctor integration validate` lists a note. An older CLI rejects these fields, so declare an `@astryxdesign/cli` peer range that starts at the release that reads them; `astryx integration verify` warns without it.
The topic keeps the base's title and description, and readers open it by the base's name.
Replace the `Overview` placeholder that `integration add` writes, or it is added to the base topic.
Extend a topic to correct or add to it. A copy made with `replaces` stops getting the owner's fixes.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Extend or replace a topic › Extend a topic

base.name: replace-or-extend-a-cli-guide
keywords: Replace or extend a CLI guide
base.description: A guide in the CLI's docs tree has a route rather than a topic name. Set `replaces` or `extends` to that route to change the guide for every app that installs your package: say what differs for your users on the page agents already read.
prose: Replace or extend a CLI guide

A guide in the CLI's docs tree has a route rather than a topic name. Set `replaces` or `extends` to that route to change the guide for every app that installs your package: say what differs for your users on the page agents already read.
Your doc stays a flat topic: do not give it a `placement`. Readers open the guide by its route, never by your `name`.
With `replaces`, readers of the route get your doc, under your package. With `extends`, each section you add or replace names your package.
A name that holds no topic or guide, such as a namespace, changes nothing; `astryx doctor integration validate` lists it as a note, with the guides below a namespace.

# Every guide route, by namespace
astryx docs authoring --depth all
astryx docs cli --depth all
# The keys to place sections by
astryx docs authoring/quick-start --index

base.name: link-another-doc
base.description: Write `{@link [provider:]kind:name}` in prose, list items, and table cells to link another doc. The CLI prints the command that opens it, so the link keeps working when the doc moves.
prose: Link another doc
Write `{@link [provider:]kind:name}` in prose, list items, and table cells to link another doc. The CLI prints the command that opens it, so the link keeps working when the doc moves.

{type: 'prose', text: 'Before you ship, read {@link generic:deploying}.'},
{type: 'list', style: 'unordered', items: ['All guides: {@link namespace:acme}.']},
{type: 'table', headers: ['Task', 'Guide'], rows: [['Ship', '{@link generic:deploying}']]},
Each link reads as a command. This link, `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/docs/extend-or-replace`, opens the next guide.

The kind is `generic` for a topic or guide, `namespace` for a docs section, `command` or `function` for a CLI command or API function, `schema` or `enum` for a schema or a fixed set of values, `component` for a component, and `page` or `block` for a template.
Name a component by its export name and a template by its id. Its link reads as the command that opens it, such as `astryx component AcmeCarousel --package @acme/widgets`.
Inside backticks or a code block, link syntax prints as written.

prose: Link another package's docs
A link without a provider resolves against your own package. To link the CLI's docs, or another package's, start the target with that package's name, such as `@astryxdesign/cli:`.

base.name: add-a-docs-section
base.description: Give your package its own section in the docs tree with `integration add doc <name> --parent <section>`. The first run also writes the section's namespace doc.
prose: Add a docs section
Give your package its own section in the docs tree with `integration add doc <name> --parent <section>`. The first run also writes the section's namespace doc.

astryx integration add doc deploying --parent acme
# Open your section
astryx docs acme
Edit its `title` and `summary`: readers see them in the docs list and at the top of your section.
The guide, `docs/deploying.doc.mjs`, gets `placement: {parent: 'namespace:acme', slot: 'guides'}`. Later runs with `--parent acme` reuse the namespace doc.
`package.json` gets the optional peer `"@astryxdesign/cli": ">=0.6.4"`, because an older CLI does not read sections; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`.

prose: Place a doc

placement: {parent: 'namespace:acme', slot: 'guides', order: 10}, // route: acme/deploying
Every field is in `astryx docs authoring authored-doc-graph-fields`.

base.description: In a topic with more than one section, search ranks a section whose title matches the query, or that names it in backticks, above words in body text. Title each section with the task a reader searches for.
prose: Make docs findable

In a topic with more than one section, search ranks a section whose title matches the query, or that names it in backticks, above words in body text. Title each section with the task a reader searches for.
Name the task in the words a reader types, such as "Deploy to production". Avoid titles such as "Overview" or "Details".
Write field names, file names, and error codes in backticks, such as `deployTarget`: in a topic with more than one section, search treats each one as a keyword.
Other words in the summary and body match too, but rank below titles and identifiers. The summary shows under each hit, so make it answer the query.

base.name: keep-the-generated-template-export
base.description: `integration verify` resolves each template through a public package path without a file extension, such as `./templates/acme-dashboard`, and fails when that path is missing.
prose: Keep the generated template export
`integration verify` resolves each template through a public package path without a file extension, such as `./templates/acme-dashboard`, and fails when that path is missing.

`integration add` writes this entry when `package.json` has an `exports` map (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/start-a-template`). Without a map it writes nothing, because creating one would make existing deep imports private. Add the map yourself, then the entry.
Keep the public path without `.tsx`. Only the target file ends in `.tsx`.
Do not point the entry at a barrel file that loses the template default export.

base.name: include-every-file
base.description: An export can point to a file that npm leaves out. When `package.json#files` exists, list the integration manifest, the templates directory, and every directory the copied file depends on.
prose: Include every file
An export can point to a file that npm leaves out. When `package.json#files` exists, list the integration manifest, the templates directory, and every directory the copied file depends on.

package.json {
  "files": [
    "astryx.integration.mjs",
    "templates",
    "components",
    "icons",
    "styles",
    "assets/fonts"
  ],
  "sideEffects": ["**/*.css"]
}
`integration add` appends the manifest and templates directory when a `files` list already exists. Add the other directories yourself.
If `package.json` sets `sideEffects`, include CSS in it, as above, so bundlers keep side-effect stylesheet imports.
Run `npm pack --dry-run` (only with npm: the tarball the registry receives) and read the real file list instead of reasoning from the workspace.

peerDependencies Libraries the copied source imports, such as an icon library. List them in devDependencies too, so the package itself builds.

base.name: run-the-package-check
base.description: `integration verify` runs `npm pack` (only with npm: the tarball the registry receives), including lifecycle scripts, unpacks the `.tgz` file into a temporary app without installing its dependencies, and checks the unpacked integration.…
prose: Run the package check
astryx integration verify

`integration verify` runs `npm pack` (only with npm: the tarball the registry receives), including lifecycle scripts, unpacks the `.tgz` file into a temporary app without installing its dependencies, and checks the unpacked integration. It publishes nothing and removes the `.tgz` file and the temporary app.
It validates the manifest, every template doc, its source file, and the templates directory.
It checks that the manifest and every template file are in the `.tgz` file.
It checks that each packed template keeps the same id, type, `name`, and `replaces` as your working copy. It does not compare template source or other doc fields.
It resolves each template through its public package path in the unpacked package.
It checks that the resolved template module has a default export.
It checks the CLI peer that features such as template replacement require.

Each failure prints a `[fail]` line with its message; add `--json` to see each issue code. `astryx docs authoring/help/troubleshooting` lists the common messages and their fixes. Fix every error, and review every warning before publishing.
base._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Templates › Build the template › Package and test › Verify the packed package › Run the package check

keywords: Know what it does not prove
base.description: `integration verify` checks the packed templates and their public entrypoints. It does not copy a template into an app or run a browser build, so it cannot show the following.
prose: Know what it does not prove
`integration verify` checks the packed templates and their public entrypoints. It does not copy a template into an app or run a browser build, so it cannot show the following.
Whether a relative helper or stylesheet survives the copy.
Whether the copied file type-checks in every supported app toolchain.
Whether package-owned CSS, fonts, icons, images, or media load in a browser.
Whether layout, color modes, keyboard and pointer input, and real content work.
Whether a template id collides with Core, or whether a `replaces` target exists. Run `astryx doctor integration templates` for those.
How the template scores on quality.

base.description: Make sure the template's styles, fonts, icons, images, and video still show up after an app copies it.
prose: Assets
The copied file does not bring sibling assets with it (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/write-the-template-file`). Give every asset exactly one owner:
Copied source The value is small, editable, and belongs to the starting point Keep it in the .tsx file
Integration package The asset should stay centrally maintained with the package Import a stable public package path
App The app must provide product-specific content or branding Use an explicit placeholder or app public URL and say what to replace
Do not make a template look self-contained while it relies on an undocumented package file or app convention.

base.name: package-a-required-font
base.description: Keep the font files beside a package-owned stylesheet. The stylesheet can use relative `url()` paths because it stays in the package, and the template imports the stylesheet by its public path (`astryx docs…
prose: Package a required font

Keep the font files beside a package-owned stylesheet. The stylesheet can use relative `url()` paths because it stays in the package, and the template imports the stylesheet by its public path (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/template-assets/template-styles`).
Ship WOFF2 when it satisfies the supported browsers. Add another format only when those browsers require it.
Declare every weight and style the template uses. Do not make the browser synthesize bold or italic because a file is missing.
Use `font-display: swap` unless the product requirement and performance test justify another value.
Confirm that the font license permits redistribution in the integration package.

Exporting the stylesheet does not publish the font files it points to. Include the font directory in the package as well (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/package-and-test/export-template-assets`).

base.name: use-astryx-icon
base.description: Use `Icon` for a standalone icon. For a component icon prop, pass what that prop accepts: most, such as `Button` and `IconButton`, take an element like `<Icon icon={BellIcon} />`, and some menu and navigation items also accept the icon…
prose: Use Astryx Icon

Use `Icon` for a standalone icon. For a component icon prop, pass what that prop accepts: most, such as `Button` and `IconButton`, take an element like `<Icon icon={BellIcon} />`, and some menu and navigation items also accept the icon definition itself. This keeps sizing, color, and accessibility aligned with the system.
Use one supported icon set consistently inside a template.
Give an icon-only control its required visible or assistive label through the Astryx control API.
Do not paste raw `svg` and `path` markup when an existing icon definition fits.
Do not render a library icon directly when `Icon` or the receiving Astryx component can render it.
Declare an icon library other than Astryx as a dependency (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/package-and-test/export-template-assets`).

base.name: understand-template-assets
base.description: `/template-assets/<path>` is a preview-only fixture path. During copy, Astryx replaces a complete static image reference with an inline neutral SVG placeholder. It replaces a complete static video reference with an empty string because it…
prose: Understand `/template-assets`

`/template-assets/<path>` is a preview-only fixture path. During copy, Astryx replaces a complete static image reference with an inline neutral SVG placeholder. It replaces a complete static video reference with an empty string because it cannot create a valid inline video.
/template-assets/hero.png Inline SVG data URL placeholder
/template-assets/demo.mp4 Empty string
./hero.png or /product/hero.png Unchanged
https://example.com/template-assets/hero.png Unchanged
Supported preview image suffixes are SVG, PNG, JPG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, AVIF, and ICO.
Supported preview video suffixes are MP4, WebM, MOV, OGV, and M4V.
Keep the preview path as one complete static string. Concatenation, interpolation, method calls, module imports, and unknown file formats are rejected when Astryx cannot replace them safely.
Use this path only when a placeholder is the intended copied result. It is not a way to ship required product media.
Astryx serves `/template-assets` only in its own docs. A preview you host must serve that path itself.

Use accurate alternative text for informative images and `alt=""` for decoration.
Provide dimensions or an aspect-ratio container so loading does not shift the page.
For video, provide controls, a useful poster, and captions when the content requires them.
Do not leave an inaccessible, expiring, authenticated, or environment-specific URL in copied source.

base.name: what-apps-receive
base.description: When several integrations replace the same Core template, one wins:
prose: What apps receive

# Receives the active replacement
astryx template shell-side-nav src/app

# Receives the original Core template
astryx template shell-side-nav --package @astryxdesign/core src/app
When several integrations replace the same Core template, one wins:
An integration explicitly listed in `astryx.config.mjs` wins over one that is only installed and picked automatically.
When several explicitly configured integrations replace the same target, the one listed later wins and Astryx reports the ambiguity.
When no integration is configured explicitly, the package listed later in the app's package.json dependencies wins. Configure the intended integration explicitly instead of relying on that order.

prose: Understand the two files

Every template has a source file and a doc file. For `acme-dashboard`, the source is `templates/acme-dashboard.tsx` and the doc is `templates/acme-dashboard.doc.mjs`. Both begin with `acme-dashboard`, which is how Astryx knows they belong together.
templates/acme-dashboard.tsx The UI source that an app copies and then owns.
templates/acme-dashboard.doc.mjs How Astryx names, describes, categorizes, previews, and resolves the template before it is copied.

The integration manifest points Astryx to the `templates` directory; it does not list each template. Change the source and doc together whenever the purpose, preview, readiness, or replacement behavior changes. No automated check can tell whether the doc still describes the rendered UI.

base.name: document-the-shared-fields
base.description: The fields below apply to every page and block. The page, block, and replacement guides add the fields unique to each.
prose: Document the shared fields
The fields below apply to every page and block. The page, block, and replacement guides add the fields unique to each.
Every field is in `astryx docs authoring template-doc`.
Set `type` to the kind you chose in `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/start-a-template`. It decides which other fields the doc accepts.

The file name sets the template id (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/start-a-template`). Labels live in the doc: the terminal list prints `name`, and JSON listings print `displayName`. Changing either never changes the id.

Write the description for someone choosing between templates. The Doc metadata category in `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/write-good-templates/template-grading-rubric` defines what a complete description covers.

Name the ideas the template serves in `keywords`: the domains, tasks, and other names a builder might use for it, in lowercase, such as `['monitoring', 'uptime', 'on-call']` for a service-health dashboard. How search and build use them is in `astryx docs authoring/field-reference`, so the description can stay about the layout.

Add `isReady: false` as soon as you generate the doc, because a doc without `isReady` is listed as ready. Keep it until the template passes `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/build-the-template/package-and-test/test-template-in-app` and the quality review.

Note: `keywords` needs `@astryxdesign/cli` 0.6.6 or later. A stable CLI before 0.6.6 rejects the field and drops that template, and one before 0.6.4 also hides your doc topics: `template --list` and `search` print one warning, and `docs` and `build` say nothing. Declare the CLI floor as an optional peer (`astryx docs authoring/ship/versioning`); `integration verify` fails until you do.

prose: Why share one

Templates help other people build apps faster while keeping a consistent visual language across products. Share one when people need more than one component to get started: a template brings the right components, layout, content structure, and interaction wiring already assembled.
Do not turn a product-specific page into a rigid component only to share its structure. Share it as a template and let each app adapt its copy.

prose: Pick a template id

Choose a stable lowercase kebab-case id, such as `acme-dashboard`. The id becomes the source and doc file name, the package export, and the value apps pass to `astryx template`. Start with your product or package name, then name the reusable pattern, so the id stays distinct from Core and other integrations.
Do not end the id with `-page`, `-app`, `-view`, or `-screen`.

Do not reuse a Core id by accident: the bare id becomes ambiguous in every app that installs your package. To take over a Core template on purpose, declare `replaces` (`astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/templates/document-the-template/replace-a-core-template`).
