base.name: global
keywords: Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user
base.description: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.
prose: Global mode

Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli
What you get
Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.
Which version runs
Inside a project The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only @astryxdesign/core, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Outside any project Your global version.
Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user Your global version, in any folder.
Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. The details: `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: `astryx docs global/updates`.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: `astryx docs global/computer-integrations`. Building one: `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

base.name: in-ci
base.description: Most CI services set `CI=true`. When `CI` is set to anything but empty, `0`, or `false`, Astryx never checks for updates and never prints a notice; `CI=false`, `CI=0`, and an empty `CI` do not count. `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER`, set to anything,…
prose: In CI

Most CI services set `CI=true`. When `CI` is set to anything but empty, `0`, or `false`, Astryx never checks for updates and never prints a notice; `CI=false`, `CI=0`, and an empty `CI` do not count. `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER`, set to anything, does the same anywhere.

Add `@astryxdesign/cli` to the project as a devDependency at the same version as `@astryxdesign/core`; then CI runs the version pinned in the repo, and nothing is fetched. A global install in a CI image also works: in a project, it runs the project's version.
Use `--json` for output a script reads; it never carries the answered-by line or a notice.

base.name: cache
base.description: When the project installs its own CLI and you install the project's dependencies first, there is nothing to cache. Astryx downloads into its cache only the CLI version a project whose own CLI cannot start needs, and, outside a project,…
prose: Cache project versions

When the project installs its own CLI and you install the project's dependencies first, there is nothing to cache. Astryx downloads into its cache only the CLI version a project whose own CLI cannot start needs, and, outside a project, the Core of a global install for commands that read components. In CI it downloads nothing in the background, so a global install in a CI image fetches that Core on its first component command. To skip those downloads on every run, cache this folder between runs:
~/.cache/astryx (or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/astryx) ~/Library/Caches/astryx %LOCALAPPDATA%\astryx\Cache
base._title: Global mode › CI and containers › Cache project versions

base.name: read-only
base.description: When the cache cannot be written, a project whose own CLI cannot start is answered by the global install, with a warning naming the folder. Point `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at a writable absolute path, or reinstall the project's dependencies. The…
prose: Read-only home folders

When the cache cannot be written, a project whose own CLI cannot start is answered by the global install, with a warning naming the folder. Point `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at a writable absolute path, or reinstall the project's dependencies. The global install's daily check and agent guide are skipped quietly when they cannot be written.
base._title: Global mode › CI and containers › Read-only home folders

base.name: short-lived
keywords: Machines that keep only the home folder
base.description: Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone;…
prose: Machines that keep only the home folder

Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error (`astryx docs global/install-once`), or run that command when the machine starts.

prose: What it is

A project's agent docs reach only agents working in that project. Your global install also keeps one skill file, `~/.agents/skills/astryx/SKILL.md`, which most coding agents read. It tells agents that Astryx is on this computer, when it is relevant (building or changing UI), and to start with `astryx search`. It names no version, so it never goes stale. Inside a project, the project's own agent docs come first.
It is written in the background on the first run and again after you upgrade, so no command waits for it. Installing the package does not write it, because some package managers skip install scripts.

base.name: where
base.description: Agents that read only their own skills folder get a link to the skill's folder, so they read the same one file: a folder symlink with a relative target (a junction on Windows, or a copy where neither can be made). Continue's scanner skips…
prose: Where agents find it

Agents that read only their own skills folder get a link to the skill's folder, so they read the same one file: a folder symlink with a relative target (a junction on Windows, or a copy where neither can be made). Continue's scanner skips links, so it gets a copy, refreshed with the file:
~/.claude/skills/astryx Always
~/.kiro/skills/astryx When ~/.kiro exists
~/.codeium/windsurf/skills/astryx When ~/.codeium/windsurf exists
~/.letta/skills/astryx When ~/.letta exists
~/Library/Developer/Xcode/CodingAssistant/ClaudeAgentConfig/skills/astryx When Xcode's coding assistant folder exists
~/.config/agents/skills/astryx When ~/.config/agents/skills exists
~/.continue/skills/astryx (a copy) When ~/.continue exists

Astryx never replaces anything it did not create at one of these folders, and never writes a folder another tool manages; `astryx doctor` names any it skipped, and any link whose skill folder is missing, as in a container that mounts only one agent's folder.

base.name: install
base.description: Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.
prose: Install it
Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.

npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli
# with Volta: volta install @astryxdesign/cli

Keep the CLI installed in each project too: that pins its version for teammates and CI (`astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`). Inside a project, whichever astryx command you type, the project's version answers. Outside a project, your global install answers with its own version, and a version you name, such as `npx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.0`, answers as exactly that version.

base.name: eacces
base.description: If `npm i -g` fails with `EACCES`, do not use `sudo`. Give npm a global folder you own, then add its `bin` folder to your PATH, or use a Node version manager such as nvm, fnm, or Volta:
prose: Permission denied (EACCES)
If `npm i -g` fails with `EACCES`, do not use `sudo`. Give npm a global folder you own, then add its `bin` folder to your PATH, or use a Node version manager such as nvm, fnm, or Volta:

npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global  # only with npm: moves the npm global folder
export PATH="$HOME/.npm-global/bin:$PATH"
npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli  # only with npm: installs into the npm global folder above
Astryx's update notice then names that folder in its upgrade command.

base.name: versions-for-projects
base.description: When a project's own CLI is installed but cannot start, Astryx runs the CLI version equal to the project's Core instead, installing it once into a cache in your home folder and reusing it. It uses npm for that, so your npm registry,…
prose: Versions for your projects

When a project's own CLI is installed but cannot start, Astryx runs the CLI version equal to the project's Core instead, installing it once into a cache in your home folder and reusing it. It uses npm for that, so your npm registry, proxy, and offline settings apply. Deleting the cache is safe: versions come back when a project needs them. Where it lives: `astryx docs global/reference`.
base._title: Global mode › Install Astryx globally › Versions for your projects

base.name: offline
base.description: Your global install answers offline in a project with only Core, and so does any project that installs its own CLI. Outside a project, commands that read components, such as `astryx component Button`, need your global version's Core:…
prose: Offline

Your global install answers offline in a project with only Core, and so does any project that installs its own CLI. Outside a project, commands that read components, such as `astryx component Button`, need your global version's Core: after any command you run online, your global install downloads it once into the cache in the background, so they work offline from then on (not in CI, where nothing downloads by itself: `astryx docs global/ci-and-containers`; and not on Windows, where the first component command downloads it). Only a project whose own CLI cannot start needs a version installed or cached; when it is neither and cannot be fetched, your global install answers with a one-line warning, and Astryx waits 2 minutes before trying to download it again (10 minutes after a second failure in a row). `astryx docs global/problems` has the exact message.

base.description: The project's own CLI cannot start, so Astryx needs the CLI version equal to its Core, and could not get it, so the command still runs: the astryx command you started answers, as before global mode. Its answers may not match the project's…
prose: "could not get Astryx … to match this project's Core"

astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the registry could not be reached); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead
astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the registry does not have it); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead
astryx: could not get Astryx 0.6.8 to match this project's Core (the release cache /home/me/.cache/astryx/releases cannot be written (EACCES)); answering with CLI 0.7.2 instead

The project's own CLI cannot start, so Astryx needs the CLI version equal to its Core, and could not get it, so the command still runs: the astryx command you started answers, as before global mode. Its answers may not match the project's Core until you fix the cause. With `--json`, `meta.answeredBy.copy` is `fallback`. Astryx waits 2 minutes before trying the download again, and 10 minutes after a second failure in a row; reinstalling the project's dependencies fixes the project's own CLI.

The registry could not be reached: you are offline, or a proxy blocks it. Astryx installs with npm, so set npm's `proxy`, `https-proxy`, or `registry` in your `.npmrc`, or add the CLI to the project and install its dependencies.
The registry does not have it: a private registry without the Astryx packages. Point npm's registry for `@astryxdesign` at one that has them.
The cache cannot be written: a read-only home folder, as in some containers. Point `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at a writable folder: `astryx docs global/ci-and-containers`.
titles: "could not get Astryx … to match this project's Core"

base.name: not-global
keywords: A global install that gets no update notice or agent guide
base.description: Astryx treats a copy as installed for your computer only when your package manager's own settings name its folder: npm's global prefix, Bun's `BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, pnpm's `PNPM_HOME`, or their defaults. A folder chosen…
prose: A global install that gets no update notice or agent guide

Astryx treats a copy as installed for your computer only when your package manager's own settings name its folder: npm's global prefix, Bun's `BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, pnpm's `PNPM_HOME`, or their defaults. A folder chosen only with a one-off flag, such as `yarn global add --global-folder ~/mine` (only with Yarn 1: uses the Yarn 1 global folder), is not in any setting, so Astryx treats that copy like a project's: no daily update check and no agent guide. Save the folder in your settings so Astryx knows it is a global install:

yarn config set global-folder ~/mine   # writes ~/.yarnrc  # only with Yarn 1: uses the Yarn 1 global folder
export BUN_INSTALL=~/mybun              # in your shell profile, for Bun
titles: A global install that gets no update notice or agent guide

base.name: core-offline
keywords: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
base.description: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once…
prose: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages (`astryx docs global`) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`npm install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
titles: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

base.name: install-problems
base.description: `npm i -g` fails with `EACCES` (permission denied): do not use `sudo`. Use a Node version manager, or give npm a global folder you own: `npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global` (only with npm: moves the npm global folder), then add…
prose: Install problems

`npm i -g` fails with `EACCES` (permission denied): do not use `sudo`. Use a Node version manager, or give npm a global folder you own: `npm config set prefix ~/.npm-global` (only with npm: moves the npm global folder), then add `~/.npm-global/bin` to your PATH.

`astryx: command not found` after installing: your package manager's global bin folder is not on your PATH. `npm prefix -g` (only with npm: prints the npm global folder) shows npm's (its `bin` folder on macOS and Linux); `pnpm setup` (only with pnpm: sets up the pnpm global folder) adds pnpm's.

`pnpm add -g` stops with `ERR_PNPM_NO_GLOBAL_BIN_DIR`, often with Corepack: run `pnpm setup` (only with pnpm: sets up the pnpm global folder), open a new terminal, and try again. Yarn 2 and later have no `yarn global`; use `npm i -g` instead.

Windows: npm puts `astryx.cmd` in `%APPDATA%\npm`, which must be on your PATH. If PowerShell says running scripts is disabled, run `astryx.cmd`, or allow scripts for your user with `Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned`.
Two installs, and the wrong one runs: `astryx doctor` outside a project lists every astryx command on your PATH, in the order your shell tries them.

base.name: both
base.description: Install the CLI in each project and once for your computer. Each side does something the other cannot, and they never conflict:
prose: Both (recommended)
Install the CLI in each project and once for your computer. Each side does something the other cannot, and they never conflict:
**In the project**, the CLI version is pinned in `package.json` and the lockfile, so teammates and CI run exactly that version, with nothing fetched at run time.
**Globally**, the astryx command works in every folder, including an empty one before a project exists, and every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx through its agent guide.

**Together**, in a project the project's version always answers, even when you type the global astryx command; outside a project your global version does. Global mode never makes the project's CLI unnecessary.
base._title: Global mode › Project, global, or both › Both (recommended)

base.name: errors
base.description: `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`: nothing can answer, such as a command that needs Core outside a project that cannot install it. When only the matching version is missing, the run answers anyway, with a warning. `astryx docs global/problems`
prose: Error codes

`ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`: nothing can answer, such as a command that needs Core outside a project that cannot install it. When only the matching version is missing, the run answers anyway, with a warning. `astryx docs global/problems`

`ERR_PROJECT_REQUIRED`: a command that only works in a project ran outside one. Commands released before global mode keep the codes they already used: `theme use`, `theme remove`, and `theme add <slug>` use `ERR_THEME_INVALID`, `integration add` uses `ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND`, `swizzle` uses `ERR_CORE_NOT_FOUND`, and `upgrade` uses `ERR_VERSION_DETECT`.

base.name: notice
base.description: Once a day, never in your first day, your global install checks the registry's `latest` version in the background, without slowing the command. When a newer one exists, a command that succeeds prints two lines on standard error, at most…
prose: The notice

Once a day, never in your first day, your global install checks the registry's `latest` version in the background, without slowing the command. When a newer one exists, a command that succeeds prints two lines on standard error, at most once a day:

A new release of Astryx is available: 0.7.2 → 0.7.3
To upgrade, run: npm i -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest

The command is the one for the package manager that installed your global install: `npm i -g`, `pnpm add -g`, `yarn global add`, `bun add -g`, or `volta install`. A global folder moved with the package manager's own setting (`BUN_INSTALL`, Yarn's `global-folder`, `PNPM_HOME`, or npm's prefix) counts while that setting names it; an app's own copy never runs the update check.
When the newest version needs a newer Node than your computer runs, the second line says which Node to install first.

Inside a project, the notice is about the project's version, and names the project's install and `upgrade` commands. The install command always adds the CLI next to Core, so a project that installed only Core gets its own CLI too, as recommended.
base._title: Global mode › Updates and notices › The notice

base.name: turn-off
base.description: No notice prints with `--json`, after a failed command, when the `CI` environment variable is set, or when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` is set; with either variable set, the CLI does not check the registry either. Unlike some CLIs, a notice…
prose: Turn it off

No notice prints with `--json`, after a failed command, when the `CI` environment variable is set, or when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` is set; with either variable set, the CLI does not check the registry either. Unlike some CLIs, a notice prints even when standard error is not a terminal, because agents run the CLI without one.

`astryx doctor` shows the same thing at any time, in its `newest-release` check, along with why the last notice did not print, if one did not. When the last check ran, and when each notice printed, are kept in `state.json` in the settings folder (`astryx docs global/reference`).

base.name: in-a-project
keywords: In a project, the project's version
base.description: The project installs the CLI, as recommended: that CLI answers, whatever its version, as it always has. When you type the global astryx command instead, it passes the run to the project's CLI, with the same arguments, input, output, and…
prose: In a project, the project's version

The project installs the CLI, as recommended: that CLI answers, whatever its version, as it always has. When you type the global astryx command instead, it passes the run to the project's CLI, with the same arguments, input, output, and exit status, so either command gives the same answer.

The project installs only Core, or nothing is installed yet, as in a fresh clone: the astryx command you started answers, as it always has. When its version differs from the project's Core, a hint after the command, once a day, names the command that adds the CLI at Core's version.

The project's CLI is installed but cannot start: the CLI version equal to the project's Core answers instead (from the installed Core, else the lockfile, else the newest one the declared range allows), installed once into a cache.

Components come from `@astryxdesign/core`, and templates, docs, and agent guides come from the CLI. In a project, that Core is the one the project installs, so component commands work offline once the project's dependencies are installed. Outside a project, or in a project with nothing installed yet (a fresh clone), they use the answering version's own Core, from beside the CLI or the cache; when that Core cannot be downloaded, the error says to install the project's dependencies. When the project's CLI and Core are different versions, `astryx doctor` warns and prints the command that brings them to one version.

base.name: see-it
base.description: In a project with only Core, the hint looks like this, after the command, at most once a day per project:
prose: See which version answered
In a project with only Core, the hint looks like this, after the command, at most once a day per project:
astryx: this project has no Astryx CLI installed; answered by CLI 0.7.2 while its Core is 0.6.8. To match, run: npm install @astryxdesign/cli@0.6.8
Otherwise, in text mode, one line on standard error names the version, unless the project's own CLI answered directly:

astryx: answered by this project's CLI 0.6.8, handed over from CLI 0.7.2
astryx: answered by CLI 0.6.8 with Core 0.6.8, the release that matches this project's Core
astryx: answered by CLI 0.7.2 with Core 0.7.2, outside a project
astryx: answered by CLI 0.7.2 with Core 0.7.2, for this computer
With `--json` nothing extra prints; every result carries `meta.answeredBy` instead (`astryx docs global/reference`):
{"meta": {"answeredBy": {"cli": "0.7.2", "core": "0.6.8", "copy": "starting"}}}

Set `calendar` on `<InternationalizationProvider>` for a subtree, or on `Calendar` itself; without it, `Calendar` is Gregorian. Values stay Gregorian ISO dates (`YYYY-MM-DD`) in every calendar.

Most calendars need the runtime's `Temporal`. Safari and older runtimes lack it: load `temporal-polyfill/full/global` there, on the server and in the browser. Without it, those calendars show Gregorian dates. See `astryx docs calendars` for the supported calendars, server rendering, and the lunisolar calendars.

keywords: Using astryx with your own i18n library
base.description: Astryx components render astryx strings through astryx's provider. Consumer components render consumer strings through whatever i18n library you already use: react-intl, i18next, next-intl, LinguiJS, and so on. The two systems coexist and…
prose: Using astryx with your own i18n library

Astryx components render astryx strings through astryx's provider. Consumer components render consumer strings through whatever i18n library you already use: react-intl, i18next, next-intl, LinguiJS, and so on. The two systems coexist and read from the same source of truth for the active locale.

Keep the two providers in sync on locale, and each library owns its own catalog. Astryx never sees your app strings, and your i18n library never sees astryx internals. Runtime locale swap works the same way: re-render both providers with a new `locale` prop and the whole tree updates live.

Single-catalog usage (where an external i18n runtime like react-intl or i18next resolves both your app strings AND astryx's strings through one provider) is on the roadmap via a `Translator` adapter. Track [meta/astryx#4029](https://github.com/meta/astryx/issues/4029). For now, run the two providers side by side as shown above.

base.description: For production apps with substantial localization needs, we recommend a dedicated i18n library such as react-intl, i18next, next-intl, or LinguiJS. If your app is small or you do not want another runtime, you can resolve your own strings…
prose: Using astryx as your i18n library

For production apps with substantial localization needs, we recommend a dedicated i18n library such as react-intl, i18next, next-intl, or LinguiJS. If your app is small or you do not want another runtime, you can resolve your own strings through astryx too. Keep app keys in a separate namespace from `@astryx.*`, and include your own `en` catalog because astryx's built-in English fallback only contains astryx component strings.

`Catalog` types the rich `{defaultMessage, description?}` authoring shape. `RuntimeCatalog` types the generated key-to-message string map. `ProviderMessagesByLocale` accepts either shape for the provider, while `MessagesByLocale` keeps the original rich-only context shape.

prose: Quick Start

Internationalization ships with `@astryxdesign/core`. There is nothing to install. Wrap your app in `<InternationalizationProvider>` and set the active `locale`; astryx components pick up localized strings from that provider.
The provider always has the built-in English catalog. Pass additional catalogs through `messages` when you enable another locale.

Astryx ships English and first-party translations for supported locales. Compact runtime modules from `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.generated.js` contain only the messages apps need; the existing `@astryxdesign/core/locales/*.json` files retain translator context. Until a locale is available, apps can pass a local catalog in either shape. Missing keys fall back through the locale chain to English (for example, `pt-BR` walks to `pt`, then to shipped `en`).
Locale catalogs only affect astryx strings. Your app can continue using its own i18n system for product copy.

base.name: text-direction-rtl
base.description: Astryx tracks text direction (`'ltr'` or `'rtl'`) alongside the locale. By default the direction is derived from the `locale` you pass to `<InternationalizationProvider>` via…
prose: Text direction (RTL)

Astryx tracks text direction (`'ltr'` or `'rtl'`) alongside the locale. By default the direction is derived from the `locale` you pass to `<InternationalizationProvider>` via [`Intl.Locale.getTextInfo()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Intl/Locale/getTextInfo), so RTL locales such as Arabic (`ar`), Hebrew (`he`), Farsi (`fa`), and Urdu (`ur`) resolve to `'rtl'` automatically.

You don't wire anything per component. Once the direction is set, astryx components mirror on their own: layout and spacing flip via CSS logical properties, directional icons (chevrons, carets) flip in place, keyboard arrow keys swap left/right, and overlays position on the correct side. Set the direction once and the whole component tree follows.

Pass the optional `dir` prop to force a direction. This overrides the locale-derived default; useful for RTL layout testing under an English catalog, or to skip derivation when you already know the direction.

Explicit direction override // force RTL layout while keeping English strings
<InternationalizationProvider locale="en" dir="rtl">
  <App />
</InternationalizationProvider>;

There's one more step: tell the browser about the direction too. Add a `dir` attribute to your page; usually on the `<html>` tag. This is what makes text align to the correct side, punctuation and mixed-language text flow correctly, and layouts mirror. The provider handles astryx components; the `dir` attribute handles everything else on the page.

Astryx doesn't set `dir` for you; you set it, alongside the same direction you pass to the provider. If your app is server-rendered (like Next.js), the `getLocaleDirection()` helper computes the direction from a locale so you can set it while the page renders:

In a plain client app, set the same attribute on `<html>` whenever the locale changes. (`getLocaleDirection()` safely returns `'ltr'` for anything it doesn't recognize, so you can call it with any locale string.)

To make just one part of a left-to-right page right-to-left; say an Arabic quote or a comment thread; wrap that part in its own `<InternationalizationProvider dir="rtl">` and add `dir="rtl"` to the element around it. Pop-up overlays; menus, dialogs, popovers, tooltips; opened from inside that region mirror too: they position with logical CSS anchor placement, so they land on the correct side and inherit the region's direction automatically.

base.name: for-contributors
keywords: 2. Directional icons: mirror with CSS, not a name-swap
3. Behavioral logic: read the DOM lazily, on the event
base.description: Astryx component authors read strings with `useTranslator()` rather than hardcoding user-facing text.
prose: For contributors
Developers
Astryx component authors read strings with `useTranslator()` rather than hardcoding user-facing text.

Astryx's own strings live in `packages/core/locales/en.json`. New user-facing strings must go through `useTranslator`; this is enforced by the `@astryx/no-hardcoded-i18n-string` ESLint rule. See the AI contribution guide for the alias-and-resolve pattern used when adding new keys.
When you author a component that needs to respond to direction, resolve it from the DOM, not from a render-time JavaScript read, and reach for the lightest tool that works. In priority order:
1. CSS logical properties first

Use `insetInlineStart`, `paddingInlineEnd`, `marginInline`, and friends instead of physical `left`/`right`. Most mirroring needs nothing more; the browser flips it from the ambient `dir`. The `@astryx/no-physical-properties` ESLint rule enforces this.
2. Directional icons: mirror with CSS, not a name-swap

Render one fixed glyph and wrap it in the shared `rtlStyles.mirror` (a `scaleX(-1)` that only applies under `[dir="rtl"]`). It flips from the ancestor `dir` through the cascade, so it works on the server with no hydration flash. Do not pick `chevronLeft` vs `chevronRight` in JS. This is how Pagination, Calendar, and Carousel handle their chevrons.
3. Behavioral logic: read the DOM lazily, on the event

For things CSS can't express; keyboard arrow-key mapping, drag/scroll math; read direction at interaction time with `isRtlElement(el)` (a `getComputedStyle().direction` check), never during render. The focus primitives (`useListFocus`, `useGridFocus`, `useTreeFocus`) already auto-detect direction from their container, so arrow keys flip for free; don't pass a direction flag to them.
4. useDirection() context: the last resort

Reach for it only when you genuinely need the direction value during render and none of the above fit. It's SSR-safe and returns `'ltr'` outside a provider (matching `useTranslator`'s silent fallback), but it's the one path that can mismatch on hydration if the provider's `direction` disagrees with `<html dir>`; so prefer the options above, which resolve purely from the DOM. As of the CSS-mirror migration, no astryx component reads direction from context at render time.
Translators

Crowdin is the preferred way to contribute; [join a language](https://crowdin.com/project/astryx), translate strings in the web UI, and your work syncs back to the repo without opening a PR. Direct PRs against `packages/core/locales/*.json` also work if you prefer that flow.

base.name: layout
base.description: Build an app layout outside-in: scaffold the regions, structure the content, tune the spacing, then adapt across widths.
prose: Layout

Build a layout outside-in. Settle the shell and its region budgets before any content exists, then work inward. Content-first layouts drift into a padded column of cards, because every section ends up inventing its own container.
Scaffold: pick the shell, budget each region, and choose navigation
Structure: rank each region's content and choose its container
Spacing: align each region to one content line, then set gaps and density
Breakpoints: decide what each region does as width changes
This guide decides layout, not component APIs. Run `astryx build "<idea>"` to start from the closest template for your app type, and `astryx component <Name>` for a component's props.

The container owns padding and child gaps; children zero their margins, and interior spacing is always a token. Pick one content line per region and hold it constant, not the padding: `container_inset = content_line - component_intrinsic_inset`.
Text and Heading carry no inset, so the container takes the full padding
List, Tab, Menu, and nav items carry a small inset, so the container gives up its padding and the component owns the line
Table cells carry a larger inset, so the container gives up its padding and the cell owns the line

base.name: rhythm
base.description: Grouping comes from contrast between tight and generous gaps, not one repeated value. If every gap is the same step, proximity does no work.
prose: Rhythm
Grouping comes from contrast between tight and generous gaps, not one repeated value. If every gap is the same step, proximity does no work.
Tight gaps bind: the smallest steps, used inside an item or field
Generous gaps separate: several steps up, used between sections
Reach for the in-between steps to tune cadence, rather than rounding everything to the same two values

Tight inside, generous between // Tight binds at gap={1}–{2}, generous separates at gap={4}–{6}.
// In-between steps tune cadence: gap={3} = 12px, gap={5} = 20px.
<VStack gap={6}>
  <VStack gap={1}>
    <Text weight="semibold">Retention</Text>
    <Text color="secondary">Logs are kept for 30 days</Text>
  </VStack>
  <VStack gap={1}>{/* next label and value */}</VStack>
</VStack>
Verify: with every border removed, you can still name the groups from spacing alone. If you cannot, the intervals are too uniform. Form fields are the exception: FormLayout owns their spacing.

base.name: columns-that-reflow
base.description: For columns that reflow on small screens, use `Grid columns={{minWidth, max}}`. A numeric `columns` is exactly N columns at every width and never reflows: `columns={4}` on a 390px phone renders four tracks under 100px wide, and the row…
prose: Columns that reflow

For columns that reflow on small screens, use `Grid columns={{minWidth, max}}`. A numeric `columns` is exactly N columns at every width and never reflows: `columns={4}` on a 390px phone renders four tracks under 100px wide, and the row overflows the page as soon as their content cannot shrink to fit. `{minWidth: 240, max: 4}` renders at most four columns, each at least 240px, and drops to one full-width column when the container is narrow; `max` is what lets that last column shrink to the container, and `gap` counts toward the room the columns need.
`{minWidth}` alone: as many columns as fit at the floor, no cap; a container narrower than `minWidth` overflows, so add `max` for anything that reaches a phone
`{minWidth, repeat: 'fit'}`: empty tracks collapse so present items stretch

A numeric `GridSpan` wider than the grid's current columns adds implicit columns to the whole grid; items placed before and after the span flow into them, and `columns='full'` then covers only the explicit columns. In a reflowing grid keep spans within the smallest count it can reach, or use `'full'`, which adds none

Styling that changes the room columns have to fit changes the count a reflowing shape reaches: a `columnGap` or `gap` step, inline padding on the grid, or `grid-auto-flow: column` through `xstyle`, which places items into extra implicit columns. A `className` rule replaces the computed track list only when it wins the cascade against the generated styles; prefer `xstyle` for overrides

Do not wrap old shadcn components in design system styles. Replace the primitive with the component that owns the behavior, accessibility, state classes, and token usage.
button / shadcn Button Button or IconButton Use Button for labeled commands and IconButton for icon-only toolbar actions.
input TextInput Keep validation state in status props rather than ad hoc border classes.
textarea TextArea Use when multiline editing is the primary action.
switch Switch Use for persisted boolean settings, including theme mode when represented as a binary choice.
checkbox CheckboxInput or CheckboxList Use list variants for grouped selection.
radio group RadioList Use when one option must be selected from a visible set.
select / combobox Selector or Typeahead Use Selector for bounded options and Typeahead for searchable async options.
tabs used as page nav TabList Use route state or current page state as the source of truth.
command dialog CommandPalette Keep app-specific search sources outside the shell and feed searchable items.
dropdown action menu DropdownMenu or MoreMenu Use MoreMenu for compact overflow actions.
alert / callout Banner or Toast Use Banner for page or section messages and Toast for transient feedback.
dialog Dialog or AlertDialog Use AlertDialog for destructive confirmation and Dialog for task flows.
card-like list row ListItem Prefer ListItem for selectable rows instead of styling Button as a row.

Mount Theme at the app root so every migrated component reads the same token set. Keep the mode in application state if users can switch between light and dark themes.

When Tailwind remains in the app, declare layer order once in the global CSS file. Load the Astryx reset and theme CSS before Tailwind utilities so migrated components keep design system defaults while legacy utility classes still work. On Tailwind v4, use the imports and layer order in `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind`.

Import the global CSS file first in the root layout or app entry, before anything that imports Astryx or theme CSS, including the `astryx-themes` module and a root component like the `AppRoot` above. Why the order matters, and what to do when it cannot come first, is in `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind`.

Root layout or app entry import './globals.css'; // first: declares the cascade-layer order

import {AppRoot} from './AppRoot';

On Tailwind v3 there is no preflight.css to import, so wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer instead. Keep utilities unlayered so existing app utility classes still win everywhere. base.name: cascade-layer-safety
base.description: In a stylesheet with no layers at all, a zero-specificity reset like `* { padding: 0 }` loses to any class selector, so most developers treat resets as harmless. Layers change the rules twice: unlayered styles beat every named layer, and…
prose: Why resets break cascade layers

In a stylesheet with no layers at all, a zero-specificity reset like `* { padding: 0 }` loses to any class selector, so most developers treat resets as harmless. Layers change the rules twice: unlayered styles beat every named layer, and a later layer beats an earlier one, both regardless of specificity. The same reset therefore wins against every component style either by staying unlayered or by landing in a layer declared after astryx-base. Same CSS, opposite outcome, and no error or warning when it happens.

This is the most common way an adoption breaks, through one of two @import mechanisms. A top-level @import without the layer() keyword keeps the legacy reset unlayered, where it overrides every design system layer. And an @import nested inside a file that was itself imported into a layer inherits that surrounding layer, so a reset can silently land in a consumer layer above astryx-base. Either way the fix is the same: import the legacy reset into the lowest layer explicitly.

Legacy reset, explicitly layered /* was: @import "./legacy-reset.css";  (unlayered: beats every layer) */
@import "./legacy-reset.css" layer(reset);
Before building screens, check every stylesheet against the cascade layer audit below.
base._title: Migration › Setup › Why resets break cascade layers

base.name: layer-audit
base.description: Audit the layers around the design system with this checklist before building screens.
prose: Cascade layer audit
Audit the layers around the design system with this checklist before building screens.

Declare the canonical @layer order once, before any @import. With Next.js (webpack or Turbopack) and other bundlers that hoist CSS imports, the order declaration must live in its own CSS file imported first, such as layers.css, because the bundler hoists @import content above the inline CSS that follows it.

Audit every pre-existing global or reset stylesheet and assign each one to a layer deliberately. Top-level imports without layer() stay unlayered and beat every layer; imports nested inside a layered file inherit that layer.
Remove or demote the app legacy reset. The design system ships its own :where() reset in the lowest layer, so any app reset belongs in that same reset layer and never in a layer above astryx-base.

Layer Tailwind preflight. On Tailwind v4, import preflight.css with layer(base). On Tailwind v3, wrap the @tailwind base directive in a named layer (see the snippet in Theme and CSS Setup). Unlayered preflight overrides theme CSS silently.
Set moduleResolution to bundler or node16 and newer so subpath imports like @astryxdesign/core/reset.css resolve.

Theme with defineTheme and the accent family API instead of hand-writing individual color tokens. Derived tokens like --color-on-accent are generated from the accent scale automatically; hand-writing only --color-accent leaves --color-on-accent at its stale white default with no contrast guarantee against the new accent.
Run the foundation smoke test below and view a few components in both light and dark mode before migrating any route.

One more mental model shift: a className or utility class you write on a component still reaches the DOM either way, but whether it overrides the component is a layer question, not a source order question. Keep app utilities in the utilities layer so they keep winning.
base._title: Migration › Setup › Cascade layer audit

base.name: core-principle
base.description: Keep the system as the source of truth for theme values. Components read design tokens from CSS custom properties such as `--color-text-primary`, `--color-background-surface`, `--spacing-4`, and `--radius-container`. Other styling…
prose: Core Principle

Keep the system as the source of truth for theme values. Components read design tokens from CSS custom properties such as `--color-text-primary`, `--color-background-surface`, `--spacing-4`, and `--radius-container`. Other styling libraries should map their own semantic tokens, utility names, or theme objects to those system CSS variables whenever possible.

Use CSS variables for ordinary DOM styling because they inherit through the tree, follow `data-theme` color mode, respect nested `data-astryx-theme` scopes, and update when themes switch. Use token resolver APIs only for non-CSS consumers such as SVG attribute values, canvas, chart configuration, color calculations, or static config generation.

For available token names and values, run `astryx docs tokens`. Focused references are also available with `astryx docs color`, `astryx docs spacing`, `astryx docs shape`, `astryx docs typography`, `astryx docs elevation`, and `astryx docs motion`.

prose: Emotion, styled-components, Theme UI, and Styled System

Runtime CSS-in-JS libraries such as `Emotion` and `styled-components` usually accept arbitrary theme objects. Keep those objects semantic, but store system CSS variable references as the values. This keeps generated classes stable while the system updates values through the CSS cascade.
Avoid rebuilding CSS-in-JS theme objects with raw color values on every mode switch. CSS variables let the class names stay the same while the browser resolves the active values.

prose: Tailwind

The Tailwind v4 bridge at `@astryxdesign/core/tailwind-theme.css` maps Tailwind theme variables to system CSS variables with `@theme reference inline`, so utility classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, `border-border`, `rounded-lg`, and `shadow-md` stay in sync with the active theme without emitting competing runtime declarations.

Pre-declare every layer before any imports. This keeps reset lowest, Tailwind preflight above reset, component/theme styles in the middle, and Tailwind utilities last so utility classes on `className` can intentionally override component defaults.

A layer's rank is set by the first stylesheet on the page that names it, so this order only holds when `globals.css` loads first. Make it the first import in the root layout or app entry, before any module that imports Astryx or theme CSS. That includes the `astryx-themes` module generated by `astryx theme add` and any root component that imports a theme's `theme.css`. If a theme stylesheet loads first, Tailwind preflight overrides Astryx base styles and theme overrides lose. If `globals.css` cannot come first, move the `@layer` line into its own `layers.css` and import that first instead.

Root layout or app entry import './globals.css'; // first: declares the cascade-layer order

import {themes, defaultThemeSlug} from './astryx-themes';

Tailwind classes backed by system tokens <section className="rounded-lg border border-border bg-surface p-4 text-primary shadow-md">
  <Button label="Save" variant="primary" />
</section>
The Tailwind bridge is the concrete example of the general interop pattern: expose another library's semantic API, but point the values at system token variables.

base.name: add-astryx-to-an-app-that-already-uses-tailwind
keywords: Add Astryx to an app that already uses Tailwind
base.description: The recipe in the Tailwind section is a whole `globals.css` for a new app. An app that already uses Tailwind keeps its own file: its `@import "tailwindcss"`, its `@theme` mapping, and its `:root` variables stay as they are. Add one…
prose: Add Astryx to an app that already uses Tailwind

The recipe in the Tailwind section is a whole `globals.css` for a new app. An app that already uses Tailwind keeps its own file: its `@import "tailwindcss"`, its `@theme` mapping, and its `:root` variables stay as they are. Add one `@layer` line above the Tailwind import and the Astryx stylesheets below it.

This recipe leaves out `tailwind-theme.css`. The bridge maps Tailwind theme names to system tokens, including Tailwind's own defaults such as `rounded-lg` and `shadow-md`, so in an existing app it changes what the app's own classes paint. Add it only when the app does not use the names it maps.

Astryx's theme defines its own CSS custom properties (color, spacing, radius, shadow, font, motion and more), and `astryx docs tokens` has the full list. An app token with one of those names collides in one of two ways. An app `@theme` key takes Astryx's value, because `astryx.css` sets the tokens on `:root` above Tailwind's `theme` layer: with `@theme { --spacing-4: 1.5rem }`, the app's `gap-4` stays 16px. Marking the block `@theme inline` keeps the app's value in its utilities. An app `:root` variable replaces Astryx's value, so Astryx's own components change: `:root { --spacing-4: 1.5rem }` widens Astryx's spacing step 4 from 16px to 24px. Where the root Theme component sets a token again, such as `--color-warning`, the app's own rules inside it read Astryx's value instead. Rename any app token that shares a name.

Put the `@layer` line above the app's `@import "tailwindcss"`, never below it. A `@layer` statement orders only the layer names the page has not seen yet, and the Tailwind import names `theme`, `base`, `components`, and `utilities` as it loads. Below that import, the statement can only add `reset`, `astryx-base`, and `astryx-theme` after Tailwind's `utilities`. That inverts the cascade: the Astryx reset then outranks every utility class in the app, and, for example, removes the borders and padding the app's utilities give its controls. Nothing reports it: the build and the browser console stay clean, and the `@layer` line still looks right in the source, so only the rendered page shows the problem.
The load-order rule from the Tailwind section still applies: `globals.css` must be the first stylesheet the page loads, so its `@layer` line names the layers first.

base.name: preferred-selector-surface-data-attributes
base.description: When external CSS needs to target an Astryx component by prop or state, combine the stable component class with reflected data attributes. The component class identifies the component (`.astryx-button`, `.astryx-card`); data attributes…
prose: Data attribute selectors

When external CSS needs to target an Astryx component by prop or state, combine the stable component class with reflected data attributes. The component class identifies the component (`.astryx-button`, `.astryx-card`); data attributes identify the axis and value (`data-variant`, `data-size`, `data-level`, etc.). This is the preferred selector surface for new CSS because it is explicit and collision-resistant.

For systematic theming, use defineTheme component overrides instead of raw CSS selectors. defineTheme keeps the higher-level `prop:value` API (`variant:primary`, `size:sm`) and handles selector generation for you. Run `astryx docs author-a-theme` for component theming.

base.name: deprecated-classes
base.description: Astryx 0.7 emits canonical `astryx-*` target classes and reflected `data-*` attributes only. Run `astryx upgrade --from <your 0.6 version> --apply --path .` to rename removed target keys inside theme `components` maps and to migrate CSS…
prose: Migrating Removed Theme Compatibility Selectors

Astryx 0.7 emits canonical `astryx-*` target classes and reflected `data-*` attributes only. Run `astryx upgrade --from <your 0.6 version> --apply --path .` to rename removed target keys inside theme `components` maps and to migrate CSS selectors. The CSS migration renames removed target classes and replaces target-qualified bare prop/value/state classes such as `.primary`, `.sm`, `.level-2`, and `.checked` with their reflected `data-*` selectors.

Removed target mappings: `base-table` → `table`; `checkbox` → `checkbox-indicator`; `codeblock` → `code-block`; `codeblock-copy-button` → `code-block-copy-button`; `codeblock-header` → `code-block-header`; `codeblock-title` → `code-block-title`; `date-input-clear-icon`, `date-range-input-clear-icon`, `multi-selector-clear-icon`, and `selector-clear-icon` → `input-clear-icon`; `hovercard` → `hover-card`; `navicon` → `nav-icon`; `popover-surface` → `popover`; `progressbar`, `progressbar-fill`, `progressbar-mark`, and `progressbar-track` → their hyphenated `progress-bar*` forms; `radio` → `radio-indicator`; `radio-dot` → `radio-indicator-dot`; `statusdot` → `status-dot`; `textarea` → `text-area`.

`input-clear-icon` styles the clear icon of every input. In CSS the upgrade keeps each old clear-icon rule on its component with `:where(.astryx-<component> *)`. A theme key cannot carry that scope, so the upgrade renames the key and adds a `TODO(astryx upgrade)` that names the CSS selector to use instead.

The upgrade treats a `components` map as a theme when it belongs to a `defineTheme()` call imported from Astryx, an object typed as an Astryx theme, or the theme object a same-stem theme descriptor (`<stem>.doc.mjs`) declares: the top-level binding exported as `<stem>`, with a static `name` and component entries that are style objects. A look-alike object anywhere else, such as a theme object from another library in the same file, is not an Astryx theme. It leaves computed theme keys, unqualified classes, unknown consumer classes, declarations, comments, and CSS inside JavaScript or TypeScript strings unchanged. It adds `TODO(astryx upgrade)` when a map has both an old and a canonical key, and when a bare class Astryx once emitted has no known meaning on the target it qualifies. Review each TODO by hand.

prose: Tailwind Integration

The package ships a Tailwind v4 theme bridge that maps all design tokens to Tailwind utility classes. Import it once and use Tailwind classes backed by design tokens: colors, spacing, radius, shadows, and typography all resolve to the active theme.
For the imports and the cascade-layer order to put in your global CSS, see `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind`.
Tailwind utilities alongside components

The bridge is pure CSS with zero JS. Theme changes (dark mode, custom themes) apply automatically because the utilities reference the same CSS custom properties that components use. This is the paved Tailwind path; for other styling libraries that follow the same aliasing pattern, see `astryx docs styling-libraries`.

Every component also accepts standard `className` and `style` props. `className` is appended after the component's own classes. `style` is merged after StyleX inline styles, so consumer values win on conflict.

className with Tailwind utilities <Card className="shadow-lg hover:shadow-xl transition-shadow">
  ...
</Card>
<Button label="Save" className="my-app-save-btn" />

For layout and wrapper styling, Tailwind utilities on className work well. For component-specific overrides (padding, colors, borders), prefer xstyle; it integrates with StyleX deduplication and the component's internal style pipeline.

base.description: Components extend HTML attributes and spread rest props onto their root DOM element. This means data-* attributes, aria-* attributes, event handlers, and other HTML props pass through automatically.
prose: Rest Props (Prop Drilling)
Components extend HTML attributes and spread rest props onto their root DOM element. This means data-* attributes, aria-* attributes, event handlers, and other HTML props pass through automatically.

Data attributes, event handlers, and ARIA <Card
  data-testid="user-card"
  data-user-id={user.id}
  onMouseEnter={handleHover}
  aria-label="User profile card"
>
  ...
</Card>

Ref forwarding const cardRef = useRef<HTMLDivElement>(null);
<Card ref={cardRef}>...</Card>

A few HTML attributes are intentionally omitted from the base type (contentEditable, dangerouslySetInnerHTML). children is not in the base type either; components that accept children declare it explicitly, so slot-based components don't silently drop JSX children.

base.name: stylex-setup
keywords: StyleX Build Setup (required for swizzled components)
base.description: Astryx components ship pre-compiled: `astryx.css` and each package's own stylesheet hold all of their styles, so consuming the published packages needs no StyleX setup. But `astryx swizzle <Component>` copies the raw StyleX *source* into…
prose: StyleX Build Setup (required for swizzled components)

Astryx components ship pre-compiled: `astryx.css` and each package's own stylesheet hold all of their styles, so consuming the published packages needs no StyleX setup. But `astryx swizzle <Component>` copies the raw StyleX *source* into your app, and StyleX source requires a build-time StyleX compiler to produce atomic CSS. Without one, importing the component throws an error that starts `Unexpected 'stylex.create' call at runtime`, and the page does not render. If a swizzled component throws that error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler. The same applies if you author your own StyleX with `stylex.create()`.
Webpack @stylexjs/webpack-plugin
Vite / Rollup @stylexjs/rollup-plugin (or a community Vite plugin)
Babel (any bundler) @stylexjs/babel-plugin + @stylexjs/postcss-plugin
Next.js (App Router, SWC) An SWC-based transform; see the Next.js note below

Next.js (App Router) is the sharp edge. StyleX's canonical compiler is a Babel plugin, but introducing a Babel config in Next.js disables the SWC compiler, and with it SWC-dependent features like `next/font`.

The repo's `apps/example-nextjs-stylex` takes the Babel path (`next/babel`, `@stylexjs/babel-plugin`, `@stylexjs/postcss-plugin`). Babel turns off SWC, so that app does not use `next/font`. To keep `next/font`, use an SWC transform such as `@stylexswc/nextjs-plugin`.
Symptom of a missing compiler: importing a swizzled component throws an error that starts `Unexpected 'stylex.create' call at runtime`, and the page does not render.
A Babel config turns off SWC in Next.js; skip it if you need `next/font`.
Pure theming (defineTheme + astryx theme build) needs NO StyleX compiler; only swizzled/authored StyleX source does.
Keep loading `astryx.css` with a StyleX compiler in place. The compiler builds your own and swizzled source only; never add `node_modules/@astryxdesign` to its inputs.

base.name: overview
base.description: Typography is built on a geometric type scale: base size × ratio^step, with 14px and 1.2 as defaults. Every text style is a semantic token that composes font size, weight, and line-height, so components express intent (heading, body,…
prose: Overview

Typography is built on a geometric type scale: base size × ratio^step, with 14px and 1.2 as defaults. Every text style is a semantic token that composes font size, weight, and line-height, so components express intent (heading, body, label) rather than raw values.

Two layers work together: raw size tokens (--font-size-xs ... --font-size-5xl) form the geometric scale, and semantic type scale tokens (--text-heading-1-size, --text-body-leading, etc.) reference them by var(). Themes override the entire scale by adjusting base and ratio in defineTheme; all semantic tokens recompute automatically.
base._title: Typography › Font Setup › Overview

prose: Font Families

Three font roles: body (UI text), heading (titles and headings), and code (monospace). By default, body and heading share the same system font stack; code uses a monospace stack. Custom themes can assign different families per role; heading inherits from body when not explicitly set.

base.name: loading-custom-fonts
base.description: Astryx never loads font files. defineTheme and the built CSS only set font-family: naming a webfont (Fraunces, JetBrains Mono, and so on) makes every browser look for it, and quietly fall back when the app has not loaded it. `astryx theme…
prose: Custom fonts

Astryx never loads font files. defineTheme and the built CSS only set font-family: naming a webfont (Fraunces, JetBrains Mono, and so on) makes every browser look for it, and quietly fall back when the app has not loaded it. `astryx theme build` warns when a theme names families that are neither CSS generics nor common system fonts and prints the snippet to add; loading the font is always the app's job.

Google Fonts: add to your document <head> <link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com" />
<link rel="preconnect" href="https://fonts.gstatic.com" crossorigin />
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Fraunces:wght@400;600;700&family=JetBrains+Mono&display=swap"
/>

Always pair a webfont with a real fallback stack (metric-similar system fonts plus a generic) so text stays readable before the font loads and wherever it never does: defineTheme({typography: {heading: {family: 'Fraunces', fallbacks: 'Georgia, serif'}}}).

base.name: line-height
base.description: Line heights are computed from a tiered target ratio and snapped to a 4px vertical grid. Small text (<20px) targets 1.5, medium text (20–31px) targets 1.4, and large text (≥32px) targets 1.25. A minimum gap of fontSize + 4px is enforced.…
prose: Line Height

Line heights are computed from a tiered target ratio and snapped to a 4px vertical grid. Small text (<20px) targets 1.5, medium text (20–31px) targets 1.4, and large text (≥32px) targets 1.25. A minimum gap of fontSize + 4px is enforced. The result is a unitless ratio stored in each --text-*-leading token.

The 4px grid matters: every line box aligns to 4px increments, which keeps baselines, spacing, and component heights predictable. The expandTypeScale utility computes these automatically when you provide a base and ratio, so you should never need to set line-height manually.

base.name: display-text
base.description: Display variants (display-1, display-2, display-3) continue the geometric progression above heading-1, at steps +6, +5, and +4. They use normal weight (400) instead of semibold, and tighter line-heights (~1.2), since large text reads…
prose: Display Text

Display variants (display-1, display-2, display-3) continue the geometric progression above heading-1, at steps +6, +5, and +4. They use normal weight (400) instead of semibold, and tighter line-heights (~1.2), since large text reads better with less leading. Use display types for hero banners, marketing headlines, and data callouts, not for document headings.

Display text often needs heading semantics for accessibility. Use the type prop on Heading to apply display styling while preserving the correct HTML element: `<Heading level={1} type="display-1">` gives you display-1 styling with an `<h1>` tag, so screen readers see the correct document outline.

base.name: dynamic-type
keywords: Following the reader's text size on iOS
base.description: On iPhone, readers pick a text size in Settings (Display & Text Size, then Larger Text), and native apps grow or shrink their text with it. Every theme does the same in Safari on iPhone, which exposes that choice through `font:…
prose: Following the reader's text size on iOS

On iPhone, readers pick a text size in Settings (Display & Text Size, then Larger Text), and native apps grow or shrink their text with it. Every theme does the same in Safari on iPhone, which exposes that choice through `font: -apple-system-body`: each font size follows the reader's choice on the curve of the iOS text style it plays, so body text scales like Body, `heading-1` like Title 1 and display text like Large Title, and every role keeps its order. A size the theme fixes at a length, such as a 12px supporting size, scales on the curve of the step it reads by default; a size in `em` or `%` follows its parent, and one that reads a variable follows that variable. At the default size every font size is the theme's own. The family, spacing, radius and the root font size never change, line heights keep their ratios, text inputs keep their 16px floor on iOS, and on Android the system font scale grows every font size through `env(preferred-text-scale)` where the browser reports it; browsers with neither see no change. There is nothing to turn on: no theme option, prop or document attribute.
Fixed-height controls such as the text inputs keep their height, so their text can overflow at the accessibility sizes. A labelled `Button` grows with its label.
titles: Following the reader's text size on iOS

base.name: typography/typography-best-practices
base.description: Do/don't rules for using the type scale, headings, display text, and semantic tokens.
prose: Best Practices
Use Heading for document headings and Text for everything else; they apply the full type scale automatically.
Adjust typography holistically: change base and ratio in defineTheme to shift the entire ramp (e.g. { base: 16, ratio: 1.25 } for editorial, { base: 12, ratio: 1.125 } for dense UI).

Use display types with as="h1" (or h2/h3) when display text is a page heading; this preserves accessibility while giving you display-level sizing. Or better, use `<Heading level={1} type="display-1">` which handles both semantics and styling.
Let line-height snap to the 4px grid via the type scale; expandTypeScale computes leading automatically from base and ratio.
Use the supporting type for secondary information: timestamps, helper text, metadata, captions.
Use accessibilityLevel on Heading when the visual hierarchy doesn't match the document outline (e.g. sidebar or card headings).
Set font-size or line-height manually; use the semantic type scale tokens so the full ramp stays consistent and 4px-grid-aligned.
Skip heading levels (e.g. h1 to h3); screen readers rely on an unbroken hierarchy. Use accessibilityLevel to decouple visual from semantic level.
Use display types for body content or in-page sections; they're designed for hero/marketing/data-callout contexts only.
Override individual size tokens (--font-size-lg) to "tweak" a heading; adjust base/ratio instead so proportions remain coherent across the entire scale.
Use raw numeric font-weight values (400, 600); reference the semantic weight tokens so themes can remap them.
base._title: Typography › Best Practices

37.name: install
37.description: Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
prose: Install
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.
Terminal pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli

Then run `astryx init` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.
Terminal astryx init

38.name: upgrade
38.description: Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.
prose: Upgrade

Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.

Terminal pnpm add @astryxdesign/core@latest @astryxdesign/theme-neutral@latest @astryxdesign/cli@latest
astryx upgrade --from <old Core version> --apply

Add every other Astryx package your app lists to the same command, and pass the Core version you had before to `--from`. If your package manager holds new releases back, exempt the whole `@astryxdesign/*` scope; in pnpm, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude: ['@astryxdesign/*']`. Exempting only some of its packages installs packages from different releases side by side.

39.name: install-once
39.description: Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never…
prose: Install once, use everywhere

Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never changes what your team and CI get. Keep it in the project as well; that is the recommended setup.
Terminal pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli
Project, global, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. Everything else about global mode: `astryx docs global`.

93.name: tailwind
93.description: The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to…
prose: Tailwind
Install pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to design tokens with no JS.

A project with Tailwind already set up needs a smaller change, which `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind` shows. For Tailwind v3, see the layer workaround in `astryx docs migration/migration-setup`.

94.name: stylex-own-code
94.description: Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your…
prose: StyleX for your own code

Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your own StyleX code. Some built-in page templates also use StyleX for layout; if you scaffold one and see "Unexpected stylex.create call at runtime", add the compiler plugin for your bundler below.
Install pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

Keep `astryx.css`: Astryx component styles always come from the prebuilt stylesheets. Point the StyleX compiler at your own source only, never at `node_modules/@astryxdesign`. Add the plugin for your bundler:
Webpack @stylexjs/webpack-plugin
Vite / Rollup @stylexjs/rollup-plugin
Babel (any) @stylexjs/babel-plugin + @stylexjs/postcss-plugin
Next.js (keep next/font) @stylexswc/nextjs-plugin
If a swizzled component fails at runtime with a `stylex.create` error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler: see the StyleX Build Setup section of `astryx docs styling/tokens-and-setup`.

`astryx swizzle <Component>` writes an `astryx-swizzle.json` marker into an output folder it owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before); every module under that folder then compiles as Astryx source, so keep copies in a folder of their own, such as the default `components/astryx`. For a folder that already holds other files it writes no marker and says how to add one by hand. With `@astryxdesign/build`'s Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, or `withAstryx()` under webpack, a copy under that folder compiles into `astryx-base`, below `astryx-theme`, so theme component overrides reach it as they reach the package component. Under Turbopack, and with the stock StyleX plugins above, a copy's rules land in your own styles, above `astryx-theme`, and theme component overrides do not reach it.

105.name: quick-start
keywords: Wrap your app in a theme
105.description: `theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported…
prose: Wrap your app in a theme

Install and add a theme pnpm add @astryxdesign/theme-neutral
astryx theme add neutral

`theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

astryx theme list --package @acme/brand-integration
astryx docs brand-theme

183.name: when-to-set-it
183.description: The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as…
prose: When to set it

The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`, when the app's own CLI answered, and otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2`.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI some other way, such as a wrapper your company ships that runs it with your package loaded. Otherwise the commands the CLI prints send them, and their agents, to a CLI that answers without your package. Most packages leave it out.

prose: How the CLI picks the command
The `cliCommand` of the packages the app loads, when they name one command.
The command a host tool names when it runs the CLI for the app. Nothing in a plain project names one.

A command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs when the app's own CLI answered, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`; `astryx` outside a project when the CLI installed for the computer answered; otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2` (see `astryx docs global/who-answers`).
Two packages that set the same command agree, and the CLI uses it.

212.name: the-tokens
212.description: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table…
prose: The tokens

A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.
{@link generic:deploying} another doc the command that opens that doc
astryx docs theme an Astryx command pnpm exec astryx docs theme
pnpm add -D @acme/widgets a package-manager step pnpm add -D @acme/widgets
npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why) a step only one package manager can do npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why)
{@pm install x} a token shown as written pnpm add x

In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
212._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › The tokens

213.name: package-manager-steps
213.description: A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
prose: Package-manager steps
A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
pnpm install npm install pnpm install yarn install bun install
pnpm add x npm install x pnpm add x yarn add x bun add x
pnpm add -D x npm install -D x pnpm add -D x yarn add -D x bun add -d x
pnpm add -g x npm install -g x pnpm add -g x yarn global add x (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer bun add -g x
pnpm remove x npm uninstall x pnpm remove x yarn remove x bun remove x
pnpm update --latest x npm install x@latest pnpm update --latest x yarn up x bun update --latest x
pnpm run build --watch npm run build -- --watch pnpm run build --watch yarn run build --watch bun run build --watch
pnpm exec tsc npx tsc pnpm exec tsc yarn run tsc bunx tsc
pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init npx @astryxdesign/cli init pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init yarn dlx … (npx on Yarn 1) bunx @astryxdesign/cli init
pnpm create vite npm create vite pnpm create vite yarn create vite bun create vite
Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.
213._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › Package-manager steps

335.name: apply-the-theme

prose: Apply the theme

Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject` only to copy source into an independent local fork.

pnpm add @acme/astryx-widgets
astryx theme add ocean --package @acme/astryx-widgets

`theme list` shows the available, added, and default themes. Use `theme use <slug>` to change the default, `theme remove <slug>` to stop importing one, and `theme eject <slug>` only when the app needs an independent source fork.
