360.name: where-it-works
360.description: Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.
prose: Where your integration works
Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.
Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.
360._title: Authoring › Make your integration work globally › Where your integration works

362.name: try-it
362.description: Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:
prose: Try it globally
Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:

npm pack  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives
pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli ./your-package-1.0.0.tgz
mkdir -p /tmp/try-global && cd /tmp/try-global
astryx discover
astryx docs
astryx doctor
`astryx discover` lists your package as installed, with what it adds.
`astryx docs` lists your topics, and `astryx search <one of your component names>` finds them.
`astryx doctor`'s `computer-integrations` check lists your package as used, with no warning.
In an app that does not install it, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command, and none of its components or docs show up.
Remove it again with `pnpm remove -g your-package`.

370.name: quick-start
370.description: An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.
prose: Quick start
Make the package

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

mkdir acme-widgets && cd acme-widgets
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets type=module  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm pkg set 'exports={}' --json  # only with npm: edits package.json
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli @astryxdesign/core typescript@6

Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.
Add your first integration item
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.
astryx integration add component AcmeCarousel

component contribution added

[ok] AcmeCarousel

Declare component root ./components in astryx.integration.mjs.

- components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
- components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
- package.json
- astryx.integration.mjs

`integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.
astryx component AcmeCarousel
You now have an integration package with one exported component.
Check it in every build (required)

Run `integration check --strict` in every build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"  # only with npm: edits package.json
pnpm run typecheck
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.
Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
Verify and pack the package

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

astryx integration verify
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: builds the publish tarball

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

`integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `npm pack` (only with npm: builds the publish tarball) writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Use it in an app
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

cd ..
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
astryx component AcmeCarousel
**Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`
The next sections explain each package field and the integration file. To build the real component, continue with `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components`.

373.name: global-mode
373.description: In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project…
prose: In global mode

In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

382.name: publish-to-npm
382.description: A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `pnpm add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.
prose: Publish to npm
A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `pnpm add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.

# Publish a release
npm publish --access public  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Or set the access once in package.json
npm pkg set publishConfig.access=public  # only with npm: Yarn has no pkg command
To let apps try a release first, publish it under `next`, then point `latest` at it once ready.

# Only apps that ask for next get it: npm install @acme/astryx-widgets@next
npm publish --tag next  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Make that version the default
npm dist-tag add @acme/astryx-widgets@1.1.0 latest  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
npm dist-tag ls @acme/astryx-widgets  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries

383.description: Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.

Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.

mkdir check-release && cd check-release
npm init -y  # only with npm: npm, which every Node install carries, writes the package.json
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

astryx doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets
The full list of commands to run in an app is in `astryx docs authoring/ship/test-in-an-app`. To help apps move to the new version, see `astryx docs authoring/ship/upgrading`.

385.name: install-the-packed-package
keywords: Install the packed package in an app
385.description: Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.
prose: Install the packed package in an app
Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.

# In the package
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives

# In an app folder beside it
pnpm add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
Install the CLI in the app too: `astryx` runs the CLI from the app's `node_modules`.
The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `pnpm install`.
Reading your work inside the package shows your source. The app shows what npm would publish.

389.name: update-for-a-new-astryx-release
keywords: Update for a new Astryx release
389.description: When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.
prose: Update for a new Astryx release
When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.

# 1. Build and test against the new release
pnpm add -D @astryxdesign/cli@latest @astryxdesign/core@latest
# 2. Rerun the checks
astryx doctor integration validate
astryx doctor integration docs
astryx integration verify
# 3. Admit the new Core once the checks pass
npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/core=^0.6.0 || ^0.7.0'  # only with npm: edits package.json
# 4. Migrate apps across a change that breaks them
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0
Run every check in `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`, not only the ones shown.
Codemod folders are named for Core versions: `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/codemods`.
Release the result as a new version of your package; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/publishing`.
titles: Update for a new Astryx release

417.name: doctor
417.description: Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.
prose: doctor()
Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.

Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
doctor(options?: DoctorOptions): Promise<DoctorResponse>
Import it from `@astryxdesign/cli/api`.
options.cwd string process.cwd() Directory to diagnose. A directory outside any project, a missing one included, gets the computer checks.

options.built string  A finished build to check before you deliver it: a project folder, a build output folder, or one built .html file, relative to cwd. Adds two checks after the others. built-astryx-usage fails when the path holds no value import from an Astryx package (any @astryxdesign/* package or an integration the project installs), no component imported from one, and no Astryx styles in built CSS or HTML. built-astryx-purity warns with the source check of astryx docs is-my-code-good: raw elements Astryx has a component for, raw SVG and icon-library icons, inline styles, classes, stylex.create and imported stylesheets, each with its file and line, in .tsx and .jsx files and JSX in .js source, found by parsing it; it is info, not inspected, when the path holds no source with JSX, such as a bundle. It reads at most 20,000 files, each up to 5 MB, skipping installs and version control; when either limit leaves source unread and nothing was found, the purity check is info, not fully inspected, and when the file limit ends the read before any Astryx turns up, built-astryx-usage warns that the rest went unread instead of failing. Given one built .html file, it also reads the local stylesheets and scripts that page links, finding a root-relative link from the nearest folder above the page that holds it; a linked file that is not there makes built-astryx-usage warn instead of fail. An empty folder fails with nothing checked, like a missing path. A source tree counts as using Astryx through an import, a re-export (export … from) or a stylesheet @import of an Astryx package; a type-only import or re-export (import type, export type, or a list whose names are all type) does not count, since the build erases it. --built goes with doctor alone; a doctor integration check refuses it. A path that does not exist fails built-astryx-usage with nothing checked, and the purity check is left out. The integrations that count are the dependencies the nearest package.json above the path declares whose installed copy, found the way the CLI autolinks (a hoisted workspace copy included), has an integration manifest. The files under the path, and that configuration, are only read, never run. Without it, doctor runs exactly as before.

doctor The diagnostic report: data.checks, each with a stable id, label, status (pass | warn | fail | info), a one-line message, and an optional fix (always present on warn and fail; some info checks carry one too); plus data.summary with counts per status.

Fail a CI step on any failed check const r = await doctor();
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) process.exitCode = 1;
Diagnose a directory await doctor({cwd: '/path/to/app'});

Check a finished build before delivering it const r = await doctor({built: 'dist'});
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) throw new Error('Not built with Astryx');
`astryx doctor` runs it. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor`.

504.name: global
keywords: Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user
504.description: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.
prose: Global mode

Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli
What you get
Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.
Which version runs
Inside a project The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only @astryxdesign/core, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Outside any project Your global version.
Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user Your global version, in any folder.
Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. The details: `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: `astryx docs global/updates`.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: `astryx docs global/computer-integrations`. Building one: `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
More
Install, and work offline: `astryx docs global/install-once`.
Monorepos and nested folders: `astryx docs global/monorepos`.
CI and containers: `astryx docs global/ci-and-containers`.
Something looks wrong: `astryx docs global/problems`.
Uninstall and reset: `astryx docs global/uninstall`.
Every path, setting, JSON field, and error code: `astryx docs global/reference`.
What each command does outside a project: `astryx docs cli/commands`.

509.description: Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone;…
prose: Machines that keep only the home folder

Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `pnpm add -g @astryxdesign/cli`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error (`astryx docs global/install-once`), or run that command when the machine starts.

542.name: core-offline
keywords: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542.description: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once…
prose: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages (`astryx docs global`) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`pnpm install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
titles: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

37.name: install
37.description: Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
prose: Install
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.
Terminal yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli

Then run `astryx init` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.
Terminal astryx init

38.name: upgrade
38.description: Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.
prose: Upgrade

Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.

Terminal yarn add @astryxdesign/core@latest @astryxdesign/theme-neutral@latest @astryxdesign/cli@latest
astryx upgrade --from <old Core version> --apply

Add every other Astryx package your app lists to the same command, and pass the Core version you had before to `--from`. If your package manager holds new releases back, exempt the whole `@astryxdesign/*` scope; in pnpm, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude: ['@astryxdesign/*']`. Exempting only some of its packages installs packages from different releases side by side.

93.name: tailwind
93.description: The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to…
prose: Tailwind
Install yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to design tokens with no JS.

A project with Tailwind already set up needs a smaller change, which `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind` shows. For Tailwind v3, see the layer workaround in `astryx docs migration/migration-setup`.

94.name: stylex-own-code
94.description: Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your…
prose: StyleX for your own code

Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your own StyleX code. Some built-in page templates also use StyleX for layout; if you scaffold one and see "Unexpected stylex.create call at runtime", add the compiler plugin for your bundler below.
Install yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

Keep `astryx.css`: Astryx component styles always come from the prebuilt stylesheets. Point the StyleX compiler at your own source only, never at `node_modules/@astryxdesign`. Add the plugin for your bundler:
Webpack @stylexjs/webpack-plugin
Vite / Rollup @stylexjs/rollup-plugin
Babel (any) @stylexjs/babel-plugin + @stylexjs/postcss-plugin
Next.js (keep next/font) @stylexswc/nextjs-plugin
If a swizzled component fails at runtime with a `stylex.create` error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler: see the StyleX Build Setup section of `astryx docs styling/tokens-and-setup`.

`astryx swizzle <Component>` writes an `astryx-swizzle.json` marker into an output folder it owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before); every module under that folder then compiles as Astryx source, so keep copies in a folder of their own, such as the default `components/astryx`. For a folder that already holds other files it writes no marker and says how to add one by hand. With `@astryxdesign/build`'s Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, or `withAstryx()` under webpack, a copy under that folder compiles into `astryx-base`, below `astryx-theme`, so theme component overrides reach it as they reach the package component. Under Turbopack, and with the stock StyleX plugins above, a copy's rules land in your own styles, above `astryx-theme`, and theme component overrides do not reach it.

105.name: quick-start
keywords: Wrap your app in a theme
105.description: `theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported…
prose: Wrap your app in a theme

Install and add a theme yarn add @astryxdesign/theme-neutral
astryx theme add neutral

`theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

Gothic astryx theme add gothic Dark-only atmospheric theme; deep blue-gray surfaces, distressed display type.
Matcha astryx theme add matcha Earthy greens; DM Sans + Playwrite US Trad type.
Stone astryx theme add stone Warm stone and slate tones; Montserrat + Figtree type.
Y2K astryx theme add y2k Playful Y2K pop; periwinkle body, holographic accents, Poppins + Crimson Text.

Every first-party package exports its built theme at `@astryxdesign/theme-{name}/built`, production CSS at `/theme.css`, and font loading CSS at `/fonts.css`. `theme add` writes those imports into the generated app module.

183.name: when-to-set-it
183.description: The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as…
prose: When to set it

The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`, when the app's own CLI answered, and otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `yarn dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2`.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI some other way, such as a wrapper your company ships that runs it with your package loaded. Otherwise the commands the CLI prints send them, and their agents, to a CLI that answers without your package. Most packages leave it out.
183._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Configuration › CLI command › When to set it

185.name: how-the-cli-picks
keywords: How the CLI picks the command
185.description: The `cliCommand` of the packages the app loads, when they name one command.
prose: How the CLI picks the command
The `cliCommand` of the packages the app loads, when they name one command.
The command a host tool names when it runs the CLI for the app. Nothing in a plain project names one.

A command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs when the app's own CLI answered, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`; `astryx` outside a project when the CLI installed for the computer answered; otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `yarn dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2` (see `astryx docs global/who-answers`).
Two packages that set the same command agree, and the CLI uses it.
titles: How the CLI picks the command

212.name: the-tokens
212.description: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table…
prose: The tokens

A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.
{@link generic:deploying} another doc the command that opens that doc
astryx docs theme an Astryx command pnpm exec astryx docs theme
yarn add -D @acme/widgets a package-manager step pnpm add -D @acme/widgets
npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why) a step only one package manager can do npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why)
{@pm install x} a token shown as written yarn add x

In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
212._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › The tokens

213.name: package-manager-steps
213.description: A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
prose: Package-manager steps
A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
yarn install npm install pnpm install yarn install bun install
yarn add x npm install x pnpm add x yarn add x bun add x
yarn add -D x npm install -D x pnpm add -D x yarn add -D x bun add -d x
npm install -g x npm install -g x pnpm add -g x yarn global add x (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer bun add -g x
yarn remove x npm uninstall x pnpm remove x yarn remove x bun remove x
yarn up x npm install x@latest pnpm update --latest x yarn up x bun update --latest x
yarn run build --watch npm run build -- --watch pnpm run build --watch yarn run build --watch bun run build --watch
yarn run tsc npx tsc pnpm exec tsc yarn run tsc bunx tsc
yarn dlx @astryxdesign/cli init npx @astryxdesign/cli init pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init yarn dlx … (npx on Yarn 1) bunx @astryxdesign/cli init
yarn create vite npm create vite pnpm create vite yarn create vite bun create vite
Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.
213._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › Package-manager steps

246.name: build-every-supported-app
246.description: Run the type check (`yarn run tsc --noEmit`, or the app's own script) and the production build in every framework or bundler the integration supports. One toolchain passing does not prove another.
prose: Build every supported app
Run the type check (`yarn run tsc --noEmit`, or the app's own script) and the production build in every framework or bundler the integration supports. One toolchain passing does not prove another.

yarn run tsc --noEmit
yarn run build
Every import resolves from the copied location.
Production builds keep required side-effect CSS.
No import bypasses `exports`, and no dependency resolves only through workspace hoisting.

335.name: apply-the-theme
335.description: Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject`…
prose: Apply the theme

Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject` only to copy source into an independent local fork.

yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets
astryx theme add ocean --package @acme/astryx-widgets

`theme list` shows the available, added, and default themes. Use `theme use <slug>` to change the default, `theme remove <slug>` to stop importing one, and `theme eject <slug>` only when the app needs an independent source fork. Applying a theme — `mode`, SSR, and the production build — works the same for every theme; see `astryx docs use-a-theme`.

370.name: quick-start
370.description: An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.
prose: Quick start
Make the package

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

mkdir acme-widgets && cd acme-widgets
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets type=module  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm pkg set 'exports={}' --json  # only with npm: edits package.json
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli @astryxdesign/core typescript@6

Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.
Add your first integration item
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.
astryx integration add component AcmeCarousel

component contribution added

[ok] AcmeCarousel

Declare component root ./components in astryx.integration.mjs.

- components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
- components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
- package.json
- astryx.integration.mjs

`integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.
astryx component AcmeCarousel
You now have an integration package with one exported component.
Check it in every build (required)

Run `integration check --strict` in every build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"  # only with npm: edits package.json
yarn run typecheck
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.
Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
Verify and pack the package

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

astryx integration verify
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: builds the publish tarball

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

`integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `npm pack` (only with npm: builds the publish tarball) writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Use it in an app
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

cd ..
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
astryx component AcmeCarousel
**Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`
The next sections explain each package field and the integration file. To build the real component, continue with `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components`.

382.name: publish-to-npm
382.description: A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.
prose: Publish to npm
A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.

# Publish a release
npm publish --access public  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Or set the access once in package.json
npm pkg set publishConfig.access=public  # only with npm: Yarn has no pkg command
To let apps try a release first, publish it under `next`, then point `latest` at it once ready.

# Only apps that ask for next get it: npm install @acme/astryx-widgets@next
npm publish --tag next  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Make that version the default
npm dist-tag add @acme/astryx-widgets@1.1.0 latest  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
npm dist-tag ls @acme/astryx-widgets  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
382._title: Authoring › Ship › Publish an integration › Publish to npm

383.name: check-the-published-package
383.description: Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.
prose: Check the published package
Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.

mkdir check-release && cd check-release
npm init -y  # only with npm: npm, which every Node install carries, writes the package.json
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0
astryx component AcmeCarousel
astryx doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets
The full list of commands to run in an app is in `astryx docs authoring/ship/test-in-an-app`. To help apps move to the new version, see `astryx docs authoring/ship/upgrading`.
383._title: Authoring › Ship › Publish an integration › Check the published package

385.name: install-the-packed-package
keywords: Install the packed package in an app
385.description: Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.
prose: Install the packed package in an app
Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.

# In the package
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives

# In an app folder beside it
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
Install the CLI in the app too: `astryx` runs the CLI from the app's `node_modules`.
The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `yarn install`.
Reading your work inside the package shows your source. The app shows what npm would publish.
titles: Install the packed package in an app
385._title: Authoring › Ship › Test an integration in an app › Install the packed package in an app

389.name: update-for-a-new-astryx-release
keywords: Update for a new Astryx release
389.description: When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.
prose: Update for a new Astryx release
When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.

# 1. Build and test against the new release
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli@latest @astryxdesign/core@latest
# 2. Rerun the checks
astryx doctor integration validate
astryx doctor integration docs
astryx integration verify
# 3. Admit the new Core once the checks pass
npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/core=^0.6.0 || ^0.7.0'  # only with npm: edits package.json
# 4. Migrate apps across a change that breaks them
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0
Run every check in `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`, not only the ones shown.
Codemod folders are named for Core versions: `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/codemods`.
Release the result as a new version of your package; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/publishing`.
titles: Update for a new Astryx release
389._title: Authoring › Ship › Upgrading › Update for a new Astryx release

525.name: install
525.description: Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.
prose: Install it
Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.

npm install -g @astryxdesign/cli
# with Volta: volta install @astryxdesign/cli

Keep the CLI installed in each project too: that pins its version for teammates and CI (`astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`). Inside a project, whichever astryx command you type, the project's version answers. Outside a project, your global install answers with its own version, and a version you name, such as `yarn dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.0`, answers as exactly that version.
525._title: Global mode › Install Astryx globally › Install it

542.name: core-offline
keywords: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542.description: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once…
prose: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages (`astryx docs global`) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`yarn install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
titles: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542._title: Global mode › Troubleshooting global mode › "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

575.description: Commands the CLI prints for you to run start with a name that reaches the same version: the project's runner (such as `pnpm exec astryx`) in a project, `astryx` outside a project when your global install answered, and otherwise the CLI…

Commands the CLI prints for you to run start with a name that reaches the same version: the project's runner (such as `pnpm exec astryx`) in a project, `astryx` outside a project when your global install answered, and otherwise the CLI pinned to the version, such as `yarn dlx @astryxdesign/cli@0.6.8`. 37.name: install
37.description: Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
prose: Install
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.
Terminal yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli

Then run `astryx init` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.
Terminal astryx init

38.name: upgrade
38.description: Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.
prose: Upgrade

Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.

Terminal yarn add @astryxdesign/core@latest @astryxdesign/theme-neutral@latest @astryxdesign/cli@latest
astryx upgrade --from <old Core version> --apply

Add every other Astryx package your app lists to the same command, and pass the Core version you had before to `--from`. If your package manager holds new releases back, exempt the whole `@astryxdesign/*` scope; in pnpm, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude: ['@astryxdesign/*']`. Exempting only some of its packages installs packages from different releases side by side.

39.name: install-once
39.description: Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never…
prose: Install once, use everywhere

Install the CLI once for your computer too, and the astryx command works in any folder, for you and for any coding agent, even before a project exists. Inside a project, the project's own version still answers, so a global install never changes what your team and CI get. Keep it in the project as well; that is the recommended setup.
Terminal yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli
Project, global, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. Everything else about global mode: `astryx docs global`.
39._title: Guides › Getting Started › Install once, use everywhere

92.description: Done. Components work out of the box — style them with `className`, `xstyle`, or `style`. Swap `theme-neutral` for any theme package (`astryx theme list` shows what's available).
prose: Plain CSS
Install yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

93.name: tailwind
93.description: The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to…
prose: Tailwind
Install yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to design tokens with no JS.

A project with Tailwind already set up needs a smaller change, which `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind` shows. For Tailwind v3, see the layer workaround in `astryx docs migration/migration-setup`.

94.name: stylex-own-code
94.description: Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your…
prose: StyleX for your own code

Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your own StyleX code. Some built-in page templates also use StyleX for layout; if you scaffold one and see "Unexpected stylex.create call at runtime", add the compiler plugin for your bundler below.
Install yarn add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

Keep `astryx.css`: Astryx component styles always come from the prebuilt stylesheets. Point the StyleX compiler at your own source only, never at `node_modules/@astryxdesign`. Add the plugin for your bundler:
Webpack @stylexjs/webpack-plugin
Vite / Rollup @stylexjs/rollup-plugin
Babel (any) @stylexjs/babel-plugin + @stylexjs/postcss-plugin
Next.js (keep next/font) @stylexswc/nextjs-plugin
If a swizzled component fails at runtime with a `stylex.create` error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler: see the StyleX Build Setup section of `astryx docs styling/tokens-and-setup`.

`astryx swizzle <Component>` writes an `astryx-swizzle.json` marker into an output folder it owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before); every module under that folder then compiles as Astryx source, so keep copies in a folder of their own, such as the default `components/astryx`. For a folder that already holds other files it writes no marker and says how to add one by hand. With `@astryxdesign/build`'s Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, or `withAstryx()` under webpack, a copy under that folder compiles into `astryx-base`, below `astryx-theme`, so theme component overrides reach it as they reach the package component. Under Turbopack, and with the stock StyleX plugins above, a copy's rules land in your own styles, above `astryx-theme`, and theme component overrides do not reach it.
94._title: Guides › Styling overview › StyleX for your own code

105.name: quick-start
keywords: Wrap your app in a theme
105.description: `theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported…
prose: Wrap your app in a theme

Install and add a theme yarn add @astryxdesign/theme-neutral
astryx theme add neutral

`theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see `astryx docs author-a-theme`.
titles: Wrap your app in a theme
105._title: Guides › Use a theme › Wrap your app in a theme

107.name: available-themes
107.description: Install the theme package you want with `yarn add @astryxdesign/theme-<name>`, then import its slug with `theme add <slug>`. The CLI imports the package's built outputs for you.
prose: Available Themes
Install the theme package you want with `yarn add @astryxdesign/theme-<name>`, then import its slug with `theme add <slug>`. The CLI imports the package's built outputs for you.
Neutral astryx theme add neutral Muted, minimal aesthetic with Figtree typography. A good starting point.
Butter astryx theme add butter Golden, buttery surfaces with blue accents; Sarina + Outfit type.
Chocolate astryx theme add chocolate Warm brown tones and cozy beige; Fraunces + Albert Sans type.

212.name: the-tokens
212.description: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table…
prose: The tokens

A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.
{@link generic:deploying} another doc the command that opens that doc
astryx docs theme an Astryx command pnpm exec astryx docs theme
yarn add -D @acme/widgets a package-manager step pnpm add -D @acme/widgets
npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why) a step only one package manager can do npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why)
{@pm install x} a token shown as written yarn add x

In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
212._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › The tokens

213.name: package-manager-steps
213.description: A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
prose: Package-manager steps
A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
yarn install npm install pnpm install yarn install bun install
yarn add x npm install x pnpm add x yarn add x bun add x
yarn add -D x npm install -D x pnpm add -D x yarn add -D x bun add -d x
yarn global add x npm install -g x pnpm add -g x yarn global add x (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer bun add -g x
yarn remove x npm uninstall x pnpm remove x yarn remove x bun remove x
yarn upgrade --latest x npm install x@latest pnpm update --latest x yarn up x bun update --latest x
yarn run build --watch npm run build -- --watch pnpm run build --watch yarn run build --watch bun run build --watch
yarn run tsc npx tsc pnpm exec tsc yarn run tsc bunx tsc
npx @astryxdesign/cli init npx @astryxdesign/cli init pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init yarn dlx … (npx on Yarn 1) bunx @astryxdesign/cli init
yarn create vite npm create vite pnpm create vite yarn create vite bun create vite
Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.
213._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › Package-manager steps

prose: Apply the theme

Install the integration, then run `theme add` with its slug and package. The command records the package owner and regenerates one app theme module that imports the built theme, production CSS, and optional font CSS. Use `theme eject` only to copy source into an independent local fork.

yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets

`theme list` shows the available, added, and default themes. Use `theme use <slug>` to change the default, `theme remove <slug>` to stop importing one, and `theme eject <slug>` only when the app needs an independent source fork. 360.name: where-it-works
360.description: Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.
prose: Where your integration works
Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli your-package`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.
Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.
360._title: Authoring › Make your integration work globally › Where your integration works

362.name: try-it
362.description: Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:
prose: Try it globally
Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:

npm pack  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives
yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli ./your-package-1.0.0.tgz
mkdir -p /tmp/try-global && cd /tmp/try-global
astryx discover
astryx docs
astryx doctor
`astryx discover` lists your package as installed, with what it adds.
`astryx docs` lists your topics, and `astryx search <one of your component names>` finds them.
`astryx doctor`'s `computer-integrations` check lists your package as used, with no warning.
In an app that does not install it, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command, and none of its components or docs show up.
Remove it again with `yarn global remove your-package`.

370.name: quick-start
370.description: An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.
prose: Quick start
Make the package

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

mkdir acme-widgets && cd acme-widgets
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets type=module  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm pkg set 'exports={}' --json  # only with npm: edits package.json
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli @astryxdesign/core typescript@6

Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.
Add your first integration item
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.
astryx integration add component AcmeCarousel

component contribution added

[ok] AcmeCarousel

Declare component root ./components in astryx.integration.mjs.

- components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
- components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
- package.json
- astryx.integration.mjs

`integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.
astryx component AcmeCarousel
You now have an integration package with one exported component.
Check it in every build (required)

Run `integration check --strict` in every build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"  # only with npm: edits package.json
yarn run typecheck
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.
Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
Verify and pack the package

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

astryx integration verify
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: builds the publish tarball

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

`integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `npm pack` (only with npm: builds the publish tarball) writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Use it in an app
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

cd ..
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
astryx component AcmeCarousel
**Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`
The next sections explain each package field and the integration file. To build the real component, continue with `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components`.

In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

382.name: publish-to-npm
382.description: A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.
prose: Publish to npm
A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `yarn add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.

# Publish a release
npm publish --access public  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Or set the access once in package.json
npm pkg set publishConfig.access=public  # only with npm: Yarn has no pkg command
To let apps try a release first, publish it under `next`, then point `latest` at it once ready.

# Only apps that ask for next get it: npm install @acme/astryx-widgets@next
npm publish --tag next  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Make that version the default
npm dist-tag add @acme/astryx-widgets@1.1.0 latest  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
npm dist-tag ls @acme/astryx-widgets  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries

383.description: Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.
prose: Check the published package
Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.

mkdir check-release && cd check-release
npm init -y  # only with npm: npm, which every Node install carries, writes the package.json
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0
astryx component AcmeCarousel
astryx doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets

385.name: install-the-packed-package
keywords: Install the packed package in an app
385.description: Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.
prose: Install the packed package in an app
Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.

# In the package
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives

# In an app folder beside it
yarn add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
Install the CLI in the app too: `astryx` runs the CLI from the app's `node_modules`.
The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `yarn install`.
Reading your work inside the package shows your source. The app shows what npm would publish.
