389.name: update-for-a-new-astryx-release
keywords: Update for a new Astryx release
389.description: When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.
prose: Update for a new Astryx release
When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.

# 1. Build and test against the new release
yarn add -D @astryxdesign/cli@latest @astryxdesign/core@latest
# 2. Rerun the checks
astryx doctor integration validate
astryx doctor integration docs
astryx integration verify
# 3. Admit the new Core once the checks pass
npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/core=^0.6.0 || ^0.7.0'  # only with npm: edits package.json
# 4. Migrate apps across a change that breaks them
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0
Run every check in `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`, not only the ones shown.
Codemod folders are named for Core versions: `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/codemods`.
Release the result as a new version of your package; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/publishing`.
titles: Update for a new Astryx release
389._title: Authoring › Ship › Upgrading › Update for a new Astryx release

417.name: doctor
417.description: Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.
prose: doctor()
Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.

Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
doctor(options?: DoctorOptions): Promise<DoctorResponse>
Import it from `@astryxdesign/cli/api`.
options.cwd string process.cwd() Directory to diagnose. A directory outside any project, a missing one included, gets the computer checks.

options.built string  A finished build to check before you deliver it: a project folder, a build output folder, or one built .html file, relative to cwd. Adds two checks after the others. built-astryx-usage fails when the path holds no value import from an Astryx package (any @astryxdesign/* package or an integration the project installs), no component imported from one, and no Astryx styles in built CSS or HTML. built-astryx-purity warns with the source check of astryx docs is-my-code-good: raw elements Astryx has a component for, raw SVG and icon-library icons, inline styles, classes, stylex.create and imported stylesheets, each with its file and line, in .tsx and .jsx files and JSX in .js source, found by parsing it; it is info, not inspected, when the path holds no source with JSX, such as a bundle. It reads at most 20,000 files, each up to 5 MB, skipping installs and version control; when either limit leaves source unread and nothing was found, the purity check is info, not fully inspected, and when the file limit ends the read before any Astryx turns up, built-astryx-usage warns that the rest went unread instead of failing. Given one built .html file, it also reads the local stylesheets and scripts that page links, finding a root-relative link from the nearest folder above the page that holds it; a linked file that is not there makes built-astryx-usage warn instead of fail. An empty folder fails with nothing checked, like a missing path. A source tree counts as using Astryx through an import, a re-export (export … from) or a stylesheet @import of an Astryx package; a type-only import or re-export (import type, export type, or a list whose names are all type) does not count, since the build erases it. --built goes with doctor alone; a doctor integration check refuses it. A path that does not exist fails built-astryx-usage with nothing checked, and the purity check is left out. The integrations that count are the dependencies the nearest package.json above the path declares whose installed copy, found the way the CLI autolinks (a hoisted workspace copy included), has an integration manifest. The files under the path, and that configuration, are only read, never run. Without it, doctor runs exactly as before.

doctor The diagnostic report: data.checks, each with a stable id, label, status (pass | warn | fail | info), a one-line message, and an optional fix (always present on warn and fail; some info checks carry one too); plus data.summary with counts per status.

Fail a CI step on any failed check const r = await doctor();
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) process.exitCode = 1;
Diagnose a directory await doctor({cwd: '/path/to/app'});

Check a finished build before delivering it const r = await doctor({built: 'dist'});
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) throw new Error('Not built with Astryx');
`astryx doctor` runs it. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor`.

504.name: global
keywords: Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user
504.description: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.
prose: Global mode

Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli
What you get
Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.
Which version runs
Inside a project The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only @astryxdesign/core, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Outside any project Your global version.
Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user Your global version, in any folder.
Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. The details: `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: `astryx docs global/updates`.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: `astryx docs global/computer-integrations`. Building one: `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
More
Install, and work offline: `astryx docs global/install-once`.
Monorepos and nested folders: `astryx docs global/monorepos`.
CI and containers: `astryx docs global/ci-and-containers`.
Something looks wrong: `astryx docs global/problems`.
Uninstall and reset: `astryx docs global/uninstall`.
Every path, setting, JSON field, and error code: `astryx docs global/reference`.
What each command does outside a project: `astryx docs cli/commands`.

509.name: short-lived
keywords: Machines that keep only the home folder
509.description: Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone;…
prose: Machines that keep only the home folder

Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `yarn global add @astryxdesign/cli`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error (`astryx docs global/install-once`), or run that command when the machine starts.

542.name: core-offline
keywords: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542.description: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once…
prose: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages (`astryx docs global`) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`yarn install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
titles: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

37.description: Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
prose: Install
Astryx requires React 19 or later: `react` and `react-dom` >= 19.0.0 are peer dependencies of `@astryxdesign/core`.
Add the core package and its `@stylexjs/stylex` peer dependency, plus a theme and the CLI.
Terminal bun add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral @astryxdesign/cli

Then run `astryx init` to install the AI agent cheat sheet (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md). It's non-interactive; no prompts; so it's safe for AI agents, CI, and scripts. Add `--all` for pointers to the theme and page-building workflows.
Terminal astryx init

38.name: upgrade
38.description: Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.
prose: Upgrade

Upgrade every Astryx package your app lists in one command, to the same release. Each theme names the exact Core release it works with, so a theme left on an older release no longer matches the new Core.

Terminal bun add @astryxdesign/core@latest @astryxdesign/theme-neutral@latest @astryxdesign/cli@latest
astryx upgrade --from <old Core version> --apply

Add every other Astryx package your app lists to the same command, and pass the Core version you had before to `--from`. If your package manager holds new releases back, exempt the whole `@astryxdesign/*` scope; in pnpm, `minimumReleaseAgeExclude: ['@astryxdesign/*']`. Exempting only some of its packages installs packages from different releases side by side.

93.name: tailwind
93.description: The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to…
prose: Tailwind
Install bun add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

The `@layer` declaration is critical — without it, component styles outrank Tailwind utilities and `className` overrides stop working. The bridge (`tailwind-theme.css`) maps classes like `text-primary`, `bg-surface`, and `rounded-lg` to design tokens with no JS.

A project with Tailwind already set up needs a smaller change, which `astryx docs styling-libraries/tailwind` shows. For Tailwind v3, see the layer workaround in `astryx docs migration/migration-setup`.

94.name: stylex-own-code
94.description: Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your…
prose: StyleX for your own code

Only needed when you write your own StyleX (`stylex.create()`) or swizzle a component (`astryx swizzle <Component>`), which copies its StyleX source into your app. The plain path already supports `xstyle` overrides — this path is for your own StyleX code. Some built-in page templates also use StyleX for layout; if you scaffold one and see "Unexpected stylex.create call at runtime", add the compiler plugin for your bundler below.
Install bun add @astryxdesign/core @stylexjs/stylex @astryxdesign/theme-neutral

Keep `astryx.css`: Astryx component styles always come from the prebuilt stylesheets. Point the StyleX compiler at your own source only, never at `node_modules/@astryxdesign`. Add the plugin for your bundler:
Webpack @stylexjs/webpack-plugin
Vite / Rollup @stylexjs/rollup-plugin
Babel (any) @stylexjs/babel-plugin + @stylexjs/postcss-plugin
Next.js (keep next/font) @stylexswc/nextjs-plugin
If a swizzled component fails at runtime with a `stylex.create` error, the app is missing a StyleX compiler: see the StyleX Build Setup section of `astryx docs styling/tokens-and-setup`.

`astryx swizzle <Component>` writes an `astryx-swizzle.json` marker into an output folder it owns (one the copy creates, an empty one, or one it marked before); every module under that folder then compiles as Astryx source, so keep copies in a folder of their own, such as the default `components/astryx`. For a folder that already holds other files it writes no marker and says how to add one by hand. With `@astryxdesign/build`'s Babel, PostCSS and Vite integrations, or `withAstryx()` under webpack, a copy under that folder compiles into `astryx-base`, below `astryx-theme`, so theme component overrides reach it as they reach the package component. Under Turbopack, and with the stock StyleX plugins above, a copy's rules land in your own styles, above `astryx-theme`, and theme component overrides do not reach it.

105.name: quick-start
keywords: Wrap your app in a theme
105.description: `theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported…
prose: Wrap your app in a theme

Install and add a theme bun add @astryxdesign/theme-neutral
astryx theme add neutral

`theme add` records an installed package theme and regenerates `src/astryx-themes.ts` or `.js` with its built module, production CSS, and optional font CSS. In a project without `src`, the module is at the project root. The first imported theme becomes the default. `theme use <slug>` changes that default, and `theme remove <slug>` removes a non-default theme.

Customize a package theme with `defineTheme({extends: importedTheme, ...})`, then build and add that local theme. Use `theme eject` only when you want an independent source fork that no longer receives the package owner's updates. For the full authoring guide, see `astryx docs author-a-theme`.

183.name: when-to-set-it
183.description: The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as…
prose: When to set it

The CLI ends most answers with the next command to run: a hint, an error fix, a Doctor fix, or a doc example. By default each one starts with a command that reaches the release that answered: what the app's package manager runs, such as `pnpm exec astryx` or `yarn astryx`, when the app's own CLI answered, and otherwise the CLI package pinned to that release, such as `bunx @astryxdesign/cli@0.7.2`.

Set `cliCommand` only when your users run the CLI some other way, such as a wrapper your company ships that runs it with your package loaded. Otherwise the commands the CLI prints send them, and their agents, to a CLI that answers without your package. Most packages leave it out.

212.name: the-tokens
212.description: A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table…
prose: The tokens

A doc never names a package manager or a runner: readers use npm, pnpm, Yarn or Bun, and run the CLI through their own. Write a token instead, and the CLI shows each reader the command they run. Tokens work in prose, list items, table cells and code blocks.
{@link generic:deploying} another doc the command that opens that doc
astryx docs theme an Astryx command pnpm exec astryx docs theme
bun add -d @acme/widgets a package-manager step pnpm add -D @acme/widgets
npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why) a step only one package manager can do npm pkg set name=x (only with npm: why)
{@pm install x} a token shown as written bun add x

In prose a token prints as a code span; in a code span or code block it prints as the command alone. `--json` carries the same commands, a `{@command}` token as the bare command that starts with astryx, which a reader that shows the doc prefixes itself.
212._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › The tokens

213.name: package-manager-steps
213.description: A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
prose: Package-manager steps
A `{@pm}` token is a verb, its names, and the flags it takes. Each row below runs the same way in every package manager; the CLI writes the reader's own.
bun install npm install pnpm install yarn install bun install
bun add x npm install x pnpm add x yarn add x bun add x
bun add -d x npm install -D x pnpm add -D x yarn add -D x bun add -d x
bun add -g x npm install -g x pnpm add -g x yarn global add x (Yarn 1); npm on Yarn 2 and newer bun add -g x
bun remove x npm uninstall x pnpm remove x yarn remove x bun remove x
bun update --latest x npm install x@latest pnpm update --latest x yarn up x bun update --latest x
bun run build --watch npm run build -- --watch pnpm run build --watch yarn run build --watch bun run build --watch
bunx tsc npx tsc pnpm exec tsc yarn run tsc bunx tsc
bunx @astryxdesign/cli init npx @astryxdesign/cli init pnpm dlx @astryxdesign/cli init yarn dlx … (npx on Yarn 1) bunx @astryxdesign/cli init
bun create vite npm create vite pnpm create vite yarn create vite bun create vite
Flags: `--dev` and `--exact` with `install`, `--global` with `install` and `remove`, `--latest` with `update`. `--exact` takes one version, never a range: only npm pins a range.
Everything after the name of a script (`run`), a binary (`exec`) or a package (`dlx`, `create`) is passed to it as written.
`{@pm install x --global}` on pnpm needs `pnpm setup` once per computer.
213._title: Authoring › Building Blocks › Docs › Doc syntax › Package-manager steps

bun add @acme/astryx-widgets

360.name: where-it-works
360.description: Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.
prose: Where your integration works
Installed in an app: it works in that app, as always, whichever `astryx` the person runs, because the app's version of Astryx answers there.

Installed next to the global install (`bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`), or in the same folder as the CLI by a tool that installs them together: it works in every folder outside a project. People and agents there see its components, templates, docs, themes, codemods, and discover source.

Installed only globally, inside an app that does not install it: it adds nothing there. When it supports the app's version and loads, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command.
Installed both ways: the app's copy is the one used in that app. In your own package folder, your working copy is used.
Astryx loads a global integration with the same loader and checks as an app's, so nothing extra goes in your manifest.

362.name: try-it
362.description: Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:
prose: Try it globally
Pack your package, install it next to a global CLI, and look at it from an empty folder:

npm pack  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives
bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli ./your-package-1.0.0.tgz
mkdir -p /tmp/try-global && cd /tmp/try-global
astryx discover
astryx docs
astryx doctor
`astryx discover` lists your package as installed, with what it adds.
`astryx docs` lists your topics, and `astryx search <one of your component names>` finds them.
`astryx doctor`'s `computer-integrations` check lists your package as used, with no warning.
In an app that does not install it, `astryx discover` lists it as one the app could add, with the app's install command, and none of its components or docs show up.
Remove it again with `bun remove -g your-package`.

366.name: fix-setup-errors

370.name: quick-start
370.description: An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.
prose: Quick start
Make the package

An integration starts as a normal npm package. Make a folder for it, create a package.json inside that folder, give the package a name, make it an ES module, then install the Astryx CLI, Core, and TypeScript for development.

mkdir acme-widgets && cd acme-widgets
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
npm pkg set name=@acme/astryx-widgets type=module  # only with npm: edits package.json
npm pkg set 'exports={}' --json  # only with npm: edits package.json
bun add -d @astryxdesign/cli @astryxdesign/core typescript@6

Set `"type": "module"`: the `.js` files the CLI generates, such as a built theme, are ES modules, and Node fails to load them in a package marked `"type": "commonjs"`, which `npm init -y` (only with npm: writes package.json) writes on npm 11.
Start with `"exports": {}`: each component and template you add then writes the public import that `integration verify` resolves.
Run the CLI as `astryx`, which runs the `@astryxdesign/cli` you installed as a devDependency.
Component commands read Core, so they need `@astryxdesign/core` installed.

The checks compare your docs with your code through TypeScript's JavaScript compiler API, which `typescript` 5.0 through 6 has. TypeScript 7 does not ship that API: on TypeScript 7, also install `@typescript/typescript6`, its TypeScript 6 API package, and the checks use it.
Add your first integration item
An integration can ship several kinds of items. Start with a component named `AcmeCarousel`.
astryx integration add component AcmeCarousel

component contribution added

[ok] AcmeCarousel

Declare component root ./components in astryx.integration.mjs.

- components/AcmeCarousel.doc.mjs
- components/AcmeCarousel.tsx
- package.json
- astryx.integration.mjs

`integration add` creates the component source, its `.doc.mjs`, the package export, and `astryx.integration.mjs`. Update the generated doc so the CLI understands the component, then write the component itself.
Read it back the way an app will.
astryx component AcmeCarousel
You now have an integration package with one exported component.
Check it in every build (required)

Run `integration check --strict` in every build (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`): a doc, prop, template, or link that drifts from the code then fails your build, not your users' apps. Set it up now, as the `typecheck` script, and run it.

npm pkg set scripts.typecheck="astryx integration check --strict"  # only with npm: edits package.json
bun run typecheck
[ok] 0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 skipped. Every check passed.
Run `typecheck` in CI and before every publish. When you add a `tsconfig.json`, put `tsc --noEmit && ` in front of the check so the same script checks your types.
What each check covers, and what `--strict` adds: `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`.
Verify and pack the package

Run `integration verify` to check that an app would see the component, then make the `.tgz` file you install next. `--pack-destination ..` writes it beside the package folder, so the next pack does not ship it.

astryx integration verify
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: builds the publish tarball

Integration package ready

[ok] @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0

4 packed files; 3/3 required files present.

`integration verify` installs the packed package in a temporary app and confirms the component resolves through its public import there (`astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`). It publishes nothing and leaves no `.tgz` file, so `npm pack` (only with npm: builds the publish tarball) writes `../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz` for the next step.
Use it in an app
Install Core, the CLI, and your `.tgz` file in a new app. The app loads your package because it is a dependency, with no config.

cd ..
mkdir my-app && cd my-app
npm init -y  # only with npm: writes package.json
bun add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
astryx component AcmeCarousel
**Import:** `import {AcmeCarousel} from '@acme/astryx-widgets/components/AcmeCarousel';`
The next sections explain each package field and the integration file. To build the real component, continue with `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/components`.

373.name: global-mode
373.description: In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs…
prose: In global mode

In global mode: users can also install your package for their computer, beside the global CLI (`bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli your-package`). It then applies in folders outside any project, and inside a project only if the project installs it. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.

382.name: publish-to-npm
382.description: A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `bun add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.
prose: Publish to npm
A scoped package is private by default, so publish it with `--access public`. Without `--tag`, npm tags the release `latest`, which is what `bun add @acme/astryx-widgets` installs.

# Publish a release
npm publish --access public  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Or set the access once in package.json
npm pkg set publishConfig.access=public  # only with npm: Yarn has no pkg command
To let apps try a release first, publish it under `next`, then point `latest` at it once ready.

# Only apps that ask for next get it: npm install @acme/astryx-widgets@next
npm publish --tag next  # only with npm: publishing goes through npm, which every Node install carries

# Make that version the default
npm dist-tag add @acme/astryx-widgets@1.1.0 latest  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
npm dist-tag ls @acme/astryx-widgets  # only with npm: dist-tags are set with npm, which every Node install carries
382._title: Authoring › Ship › Publish an integration › Publish to npm

383.name: check-the-published-package
383.description: Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.
prose: Check the published package
Install the version you published in a clean app, and run the same commands you ran against the `.tgz` file.

mkdir check-release && cd check-release
npm init -y  # only with npm: npm, which every Node install carries, writes the package.json
bun add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli @acme/astryx-widgets@1.0.0
astryx component AcmeCarousel
astryx doctor integration validate @acme/astryx-widgets
The full list of commands to run in an app is in `astryx docs authoring/ship/test-in-an-app`. To help apps move to the new version, see `astryx docs authoring/ship/upgrading`.

385.name: install-the-packed-package
keywords: Install the packed package in an app
385.description: Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.
prose: Install the packed package in an app
Pack the package beside its folder, so the next pack does not ship it, then install it in an app together with Core and the CLI. The app loads your package because it is a dependency.

# In the package
npm pack --pack-destination ..  # only with npm: the tarball the registry receives

# In an app folder beside it
bun add @astryxdesign/core @astryxdesign/cli ../acme-astryx-widgets-1.0.0.tgz
Install the CLI in the app too: `astryx` runs the CLI from the app's `node_modules`.
The app holds a copy, not a link. After each change, pack again and run the same `bun install`.
Reading your work inside the package shows your source. The app shows what npm would publish.

389.name: update-for-a-new-astryx-release
keywords: Update for a new Astryx release
389.description: When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.
prose: Update for a new Astryx release
When Astryx ships a release, bump your devDependencies, rerun the checks, widen your peer ranges, and ship a codemod for each change that breaks apps.

# 1. Build and test against the new release
bun add -d @astryxdesign/cli@latest @astryxdesign/core@latest
# 2. Rerun the checks
astryx doctor integration validate
astryx doctor integration docs
astryx integration verify
# 3. Admit the new Core once the checks pass
npm pkg set 'peerDependencies.@astryxdesign/core=^0.6.0 || ^0.7.0'  # only with npm: edits package.json
# 4. Migrate apps across a change that breaks them
astryx integration add codemod rename-delay --to 0.7.0
Run every check in `astryx docs authoring/ship/checks`, not only the ones shown.
Codemod folders are named for Core versions: `astryx docs authoring/building-blocks/codemods`.
Release the result as a new version of your package; see `astryx docs authoring/ship/publishing`.
titles: Update for a new Astryx release
389._title: Authoring › Ship › Upgrading › Update for a new Astryx release

417.name: doctor
417.description: Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.
prose: doctor()
Check a project's Astryx setup and get a pass/warn/fail report per check. Use it as a CI gate or before debugging a broken install.

Runs a series of diagnostics: Node version, @astryxdesign/core install and version alignment with the CLI, installed themes and wiring, astryx.config validity, whether every integration astryx.config names loads (a failed one fails the run), integrations linked from package.json without a config entry, core peer dependencies, integration provider identity and contribution issues, agent docs, the detected package manager, and the health of the docs the CLI reads (authoring and CLI docs, the docs tree, doc size), and returns a structured report. Theme checks run when the generated app module exists; without one, doctor reports that the CLI manages no themes and names theme add, and the `themes` check counts a theme as wired when package.json `astryx.theme` names one or when the source of the app (JavaScript, TypeScript and CSS files, outside dependencies and build output; type-only imports do not count) imports the built module or stylesheet of a discovered theme, the same imports theme add writes, or passes one to Theme (followed through module-scope variables, defineTheme extends, re-exports and installed packages; only a theme whose package is installed, or a local theme, counts), naming the file; a theme passed to Theme that cannot be traced, such as a prop or a variable declared inside a component, is reported as unconfirmed (info), not as missing. Earlier descriptor-less copies are a non-failing upgrade warning. It never installs, writes, or mutates. It imports astryx.config, executes every added theme source while validating private inputs, and loads every recorded built theme module to prove its runtime imports work, including themes from installed packages. Local theme source also runs during build-freshness checks. Stylesheets are parsed without execution. Config and theme top-level code therefore run, so use doctor only with project code you trust. Outside a project it checks the computer instead: the Node version (`node-version`), the release that answered (`answering-release`), the newest release the computer knows of (`newest-release`), the astryx commands on the search path (`cli-on-path`), the integrations installed for the computer (`computer-integrations`: each one used outside a project, and a warning for one skipped because its peer range excludes the answering release or that fails to load), and the computer-level agent text (`computer-agent-text`): present and matching this release, present but different, edited, absent, or turned off, and where it is linked, with `astryx init --user` as the fix for the stale and absent cases. The agent-text check is always info. The newest-release check also runs inside a project: it names a newer release when the computer knows of one; inside a project whose release is older it names the install and upgrade commands; outside one, when the CLI installed for the computer is older, it names the command of the package manager that installed it, after the Node the newest release needs when the computer runs an older one. It is always info and installs nothing. The `cli-on-path` check also runs inside a project: it lists every astryx command on the search path in order, passes when the first is a release that hands each project run to the release of that project, and warns when the first is another program or a release that predates the hand-off, naming `bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli@latest`. Inside a project, `computer-integrations` lists, as info, the integrations installed for the computer that the project does not install, with its install command; they are not used there. It never fails a check because the folder has no project, and installs nothing. In global mode: with `cwd` outside a project, it checks the computer instead (the Node version, the version that answered, the newest version it knows of, the astryx commands on the search path, the integrations installed globally, and the agent guide for the computer) and never fails a check because the folder has no project. See `astryx docs global` and `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
doctor(options?: DoctorOptions): Promise<DoctorResponse>
Import it from `@astryxdesign/cli/api`.
options.cwd string process.cwd() Directory to diagnose. A directory outside any project, a missing one included, gets the computer checks.

options.built string  A finished build to check before you deliver it: a project folder, a build output folder, or one built .html file, relative to cwd. Adds two checks after the others. built-astryx-usage fails when the path holds no value import from an Astryx package (any @astryxdesign/* package or an integration the project installs), no component imported from one, and no Astryx styles in built CSS or HTML. built-astryx-purity warns with the source check of astryx docs is-my-code-good: raw elements Astryx has a component for, raw SVG and icon-library icons, inline styles, classes, stylex.create and imported stylesheets, each with its file and line, in .tsx and .jsx files and JSX in .js source, found by parsing it; it is info, not inspected, when the path holds no source with JSX, such as a bundle. It reads at most 20,000 files, each up to 5 MB, skipping installs and version control; when either limit leaves source unread and nothing was found, the purity check is info, not fully inspected, and when the file limit ends the read before any Astryx turns up, built-astryx-usage warns that the rest went unread instead of failing. Given one built .html file, it also reads the local stylesheets and scripts that page links, finding a root-relative link from the nearest folder above the page that holds it; a linked file that is not there makes built-astryx-usage warn instead of fail. An empty folder fails with nothing checked, like a missing path. A source tree counts as using Astryx through an import, a re-export (export … from) or a stylesheet @import of an Astryx package; a type-only import or re-export (import type, export type, or a list whose names are all type) does not count, since the build erases it. --built goes with doctor alone; a doctor integration check refuses it. A path that does not exist fails built-astryx-usage with nothing checked, and the purity check is left out. The integrations that count are the dependencies the nearest package.json above the path declares whose installed copy, found the way the CLI autolinks (a hoisted workspace copy included), has an integration manifest. The files under the path, and that configuration, are only read, never run. Without it, doctor runs exactly as before.

doctor The diagnostic report: data.checks, each with a stable id, label, status (pass | warn | fail | info), a one-line message, and an optional fix (always present on warn and fail; some info checks carry one too); plus data.summary with counts per status.

Fail a CI step on any failed check const r = await doctor();
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) process.exitCode = 1;
Diagnose a directory await doctor({cwd: '/path/to/app'});

Check a finished build before delivering it const r = await doctor({built: 'dist'});
if (r.data.summary.fail > 0) throw new Error('Not built with Astryx');
`astryx doctor` runs it. Read it with `astryx docs cli/commands/doctor`.

504.name: global
keywords: Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user
504.description: Install Astryx once on your computer and use it in any folder. Each project still runs its own version of Astryx, so a global install never changes what a project gets.
prose: Global mode

Global mode means installing the Astryx CLI once for your computer, so the astryx command works everywhere: in your projects, in an empty folder, and for every coding agent. Inside a project, the project's own version of Astryx answers, so your global install never changes what a project gets.
bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli
What you get
Docs, components, templates, and search in any folder, before you have a project.
Every coding agent on your computer knows Astryx, through a short guide the CLI keeps where agent tools look.
Each project keeps its own version: in a project, the project's version answers, whichever astryx command you run.
Which version runs
Inside a project The project's own CLI. In a project that installs only @astryxdesign/core, the astryx command you started, with a hint once a day to add the CLI.
Outside any project Your global version.
Commands for your computer, such as astryx init --user Your global version, in any folder.
Not sure whether you want a project install, a global one, or both: `astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`. The details: `astryx docs global/who-answers`.
Updates
Your global install never upgrades itself or a project. When a newer version is out, a command that succeeds ends with a two-line notice, at most once a day: `astryx docs global/updates`.
Agents
The CLI keeps a short Astryx guide where agent tools look in your home folder, so an agent working anywhere knows Astryx is there: `astryx docs global/computer-agent-guide`.
Integrations

Integrations you install next to your global install work outside projects. Inside a project, only the project's own integrations do: `astryx docs global/computer-integrations`. Building one: `astryx docs authoring/global-integrations`.
More
Install, and work offline: `astryx docs global/install-once`.
Monorepos and nested folders: `astryx docs global/monorepos`.
CI and containers: `astryx docs global/ci-and-containers`.
Something looks wrong: `astryx docs global/problems`.
Uninstall and reset: `astryx docs global/uninstall`.
Every path, setting, JSON field, and error code: `astryx docs global/reference`.
What each command does outside a project: `astryx docs cli/commands`.

509.name: short-lived
keywords: Machines that keep only the home folder
509.description: Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone;…
prose: Machines that keep only the home folder

Some agent machines keep the home folder across restarts but not system folders. A global install there disappears on restart while the agent guide in the home folder stays, so agents are told to run a global astryx command that is gone; the guide says to run the command that installed the CLI, such as `bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli`, when that command is not found, and `astryx doctor` names the same step. To keep the CLI across restarts, install it into a folder in your home and put its `bin` folder on your PATH, as for a permission error (`astryx docs global/install-once`), or run that command when the machine starts.
titles: Machines that keep only the home folder
509._title: Global mode › CI and containers › Machines that keep only the home folder

525.description: Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.

Install the CLI package with your package manager. One astryx command then works in every folder.

bun add -g @astryxdesign/cli

Keep the CLI installed in each project too: that pins its version for teammates and CI (`astryx docs global/project-global-or-both`). 542.name: core-offline
keywords: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542.description: Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once…
prose: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

Outside a project, commands that read components (`component`, `search`, `template`, `build`, and the like) use your global version's Core. It ships beside the CLI only for some installs; otherwise your global install downloads it once into its cache in the background after a command you run online (on Windows, the first component command downloads it), and a component command before that, offline, fails with `ERR_VERSIONS_UNAVAILABLE`. Reinstalling the CLI does not help: run any command once online, and component reads work offline from then on. In CI nothing downloads in the background, so the first component command there needs the registry. The global-mode pages (`astryx docs global`) read offline either way.

In a project with nothing installed yet, such as a fresh clone, the same commands use that Core too, and offline the error reads `This project has no Core installed, and Core <version> could not be downloaded`: install the project's dependencies (`bun install`, or your package manager's), and the project's own Core answers from then on.
titles: "Core … could not be installed" outside a project
542._title: Global mode › Troubleshooting global mode › "Core … could not be installed" outside a project

templates.name: BreadcrumbItemShowcase

templates.name: BreadcrumbsCustomSeparator

templates.name: BreadcrumbsSupportingVariant

templates.name: ButtonWithEndSlot

templates.name: ButtonFloating

templates.name: ButtonWithIcon

templates.name: ButtonGroupBasic

templates.name: ButtonGroupFloating

templates.name: ChatComposerAttachments

templates.name: ChatComposerFooterActions

templates.name: ChatComposerFullFeatured

templates.name: ChatComposerSimple
templates.description: Minimal chat composer with a placeholder and submit handler. The simplest way to drop a message input into a page.

templates.name: ChatComposerStreaming
templates.description: Chat composer with streaming state and a stop button. Use when the assistant is generating a response and the user can cancel.

templates.name: ChatComposerValidation

templates.name: ChatComposerDrawerShowcase
templates.description: Composer drawer with file tokens, a collapsible toggle, and header actions. Use as a starting point for any chat composer with attachments.

templates.name: ChatComposerDrawerFeedback

templates.name: ChatComposerDrawerWithProgress

templates.name: StepShowcase
templates.description: A single Step, with every part it can render: the indicator, the label with its optional marker and trailing endContent, and the description beneath. A Step never sets its own completed/current state. It declares its index and derives the rest from the parent Stepper, so one Step in one Stepper is a complete example.

templates.name: StepContent
templates.description: Children passed to a Step render below its description, indented to line up with the label rather than the indicator, and stay outside the clickable label area so buttons inside remain their own targets. In a full flow you gate the slot on the step being active. That is what turns a vertical stepper into an expanding one.

templates.name: StepIndicator
templates.description: Everything the indicator prop accepts: the auto default, an always-number badge, a custom ReactNode, and none, each on its own completed Step so the prop is the only difference between them. Every variant occupies the same 16px box, so a step swapping its number for a check as it completes never shifts the label beside it. The last cell shows that a custom node can be live rather than static: a Spinner on a step that is in progress, shaded `inherit` so it picks up the step's own tint like any other glyph.

templates.name: StepStates
templates.description: Every state a single Step can land in, each shown as one Step in its own Stepper. Completed, current, and upcoming are derived by comparing the step index against the parent activeStep, so they are never set directly; isDisabled and status are the two a step declares itself. Status is a separate axis from progress, which is why a completed step can still carry a warning.

templates.name: StepperShowcase
templates.description: The default stepper: a horizontal track where every step owns an equal segment of the progress bar above its label. The default auto indicator resolves itself per step: a check once the step is done, a ring on the current step, a number for the ones still ahead. Click any step to jump.

templates.name: StepperCustomContent
templates.description: A vertical stepper where each step owns a slice of the page. The content slot takes any node (form fields, a summary panel, a banner), so a stepper is not limited to multi-step forms. Rendering the slot only for the active step is what makes the flow expand one step at a time.

templates.name: StepperWidthResponsiveCollapse
templates.description: A narrow horizontal stepper using horizontalOptions. At 320px wide, four steps fall below the 112px minimumStepWidth and collapse into a current-step summary with Previous and Next controls.

templates.name: StepperIndicatorModes
templates.description: The indicator prop side by side: none (the bar and label carry the progress on their own), auto (check when done, ring when current, number ahead), always-number, and a custom icon per step.

templates.name: StepperOnTrackHorizontal
templates.description: The on-track layout in horizontal orientation: instead of sitting beside the label, each indicator is slotted into the connector itself, so the numbered nodes read as beads on one continuous line. Labels center under their node.

templates.name: StepperOnTrackVertical
templates.description: The on-track layout in vertical orientation: indicators sit inline on a continuous connector rail, with each label and description beside its node. Compare with the separated layout, where the indicator sits alongside its own bar segment instead of on a shared rail.

templates.name: TabListTabsWithStatusDot

templates.name: TabMenuBasic

templates.name: TextWrap

templates.name: TextInputIcon

templates.name: TextInputSearch

templates.name: TextInputSizes

templates.name: TextInputStates
templates.description: Error, warning, and success validation states with status messages. Use to show users what went wrong and how to fix it.

templates.name: TextInputTypes
templates.description: Text, password, and email types plus field-level features: tooltip, required, optional, description, disabled, and loading.

templates.name: ThumbnailShowcase
templates.description: A thumbnail with an image and label.

templates.name: ThumbnailDisabled
templates.description: Thumbnails in the disabled state with reduced opacity. The open and remove buttons stay focusable and announced as disabled, and call nothing.

templates.name: ThumbnailGallery
templates.description: A row of clickable thumbnails with labels that open a detail view. Use for image attachment lists where users need to preview and manage uploads.

templates.name: ThumbnailRemovable
templates.description: Thumbnails with a remove button overlay. The close button uses APCA luminance detection to stay visible on both dark and light images.

templates.name: ThumbnailStates
templates.description: All visual states side by side: image loaded, placeholder, skeleton loading, and upload overlay. Demonstrates the full lifecycle of a thumbnail from empty to loaded.

templates.name: TimeInputShowcase
templates.description: A time input that uses the browser/OS picker on touch by default and Astryx typed entry on fine pointers.

templates.name: TimeInputConstrained
templates.description: Time inputs with min/max constraints limiting selection to specific windows. Use to prevent out-of-bounds selections for appointments, reservations, or shift scheduling.

templates.name: TimeInputFormats
templates.description: 12-hour, 24-hour, and seconds formats side by side. Use 12h for US-centric UIs, 24h for international or technical contexts, and seconds for precise timing.

templates.name: TimeInputIncrement
templates.description: Time input with a custom step increment. Arrow keys jump by the specified interval (e.g. 15 minutes) for quick slot-based scheduling.

templates.name: TimeInputStates
templates.description: Default, disabled, error, warning, and success states. Use status messages to give users clear feedback about their time selection.

templates.name: TimerFormats
templates.description: Elapsed compact units and stopwatch clock notation shown from the same start time.

templates.name: TimerInline
templates.description: A Timer composed into status copy while inheriting the surrounding typography.

templates.name: TimerTypography
templates.description: Timer using its Timestamp-matched default typography and an emphasized override.

templates.name: TimestampAutoFormat
templates.description: Auto format that shows relative time for recent dates and switches to the full date for older ones. The default choice for most use cases.

templates.name: TimestampColors
templates.description: Timestamp rendered in each available color variant: primary, secondary, disabled, and active.

templates.name: TimestampFormats
templates.description: All display formats side by side: date, date_time, time, and their system equivalents. Use date and date_time for user-facing UI, system variants for logs and dev tools.

templates.name: TimestampRelativeFormat
templates.description: Relative time labels from seconds to months ago, with hover tooltips showing the full date. Use in feeds, comment threads, and activity logs.

templates.name: TimestampTimezone
templates.description: Timestamps with the timezone abbreviation appended. Enable isTimezoneShown for audiences across time zones, like audit logs or team calendars.

templates.name: TimestampTooltipTimezones
templates.description: Hover tooltips that show one instant across several time zones or formats. Use tooltipEntries when readers must compare zones, like an incident log carrying both the reader's time and the event's origin zone.

templates.name: ToastShowcase
templates.description: Imperative toast notifications triggered with useToast and rendered in the toast viewport.

templates.name: ToastAction
templates.description: Persistent toasts with a trailing button or link so the user can act on the notification, like undoing a delete or viewing a report.

templates.name: ToastDeduplication
templates.description: Prevent duplicate toasts with uniqueID. Use ignore to keep the first toast, or overwrite to replace it with updated content like a progress percentage.

templates.name: ToastDismiss
templates.description: Show a persistent toast and dismiss it programmatically using the function returned by useToast. Use for long-running operations that need manual cleanup.

templates.name: ToastStacking
templates.description: Multiple toasts stacking vertically with smooth enter and exit animations. Click repeatedly to see how toasts queue and dismiss.

templates.name: ToastTypes
templates.description: Info and error toast variants side by side. Info toasts auto-dismiss after 5 seconds, error toasts persist until the user dismisses them.

templates.name: ToggleButtonColor
templates.description: Toggle buttons with colored icons in the pressed state. Shows accent-colored toolbar formatting and semantic reaction colors (yellow star, red heart, blue bookmark).

templates.name: ToggleButtonGroup
templates.description: Toggle button groups in single-select and multi-select modes. Single selection acts as a view mode switcher; multiple selection forms a formatting toolbar.

templates.name: ToggleButtonIconSwap
templates.description: Icon-only toggle buttons that swap between outline and solid icons when pressed. Use for actions like favorite, bookmark, or mute where the icon itself communicates the state.

templates.name: ToggleButtonLabel
templates.description: Toggle buttons with visible text labels that show a font weight shift on press. Use when the icon alone is not enough to communicate the action.

templates.name: ToggleButtonStates
templates.description: Default, pressed, disabled, and loading states of a standalone toggle button. Shows how visual treatment changes across states.

templates.name: ToggleButtonGroupShowcase
templates.description: ToggleButtonGroup manages a set of ToggleButtons with single-select or multi-select behavior for options like view modes or filters.

templates.name: ToggleButtonGroupVertical
templates.description: A vertically stacked ToggleButtonGroup using the vertical orientation, shown with both single-select and multi-select behavior, ideal for sidebar-style option lists and vertical toolbars.

templates.name: TokenClickable
templates.description: Interactive tokens that respond to clicks. Use for toggleable filters or tokens that open a detail view when selected.

templates.name: TokenColors
templates.description: All 11 color variants in default and disabled states. Use color to categorize entities or convey status at a glance.

templates.name: TokenEndContent
templates.description: Tokens with trailing content like a count badge or status indicator after the label. Use for notification counts, item quantities, or compact status info.

templates.name: TokenIcon
templates.description: Tokens with a leading icon that identifies the entity type. Use when the icon helps users recognize the token category faster, like a user icon for people or a tag icon for labels.

templates.name: TokenRemovable
templates.description: Tokens with a dismiss button for selections the user can undo. Use in multi-select fields, active filters, or any list of user-chosen items.

templates.name: TokenizerShowcase
templates.description: A tokenizer with preset tags and search source.

templates.name: TokenizerClear
templates.description: Tokenizer with a built-in clear-all button for bulk removal of all selected tokens. On touch screens, clear through the sheet's Clear all.

templates.name: TokenizerCreatable
templates.description: Free-text tokenizer for creating custom tags and a combined create-or-search pattern. Use when users need to enter values that may not exist in a predefined list.

templates.name: TokenizerEndContent
templates.description: Tokenizer with an action button in the end slot. Use for inline actions like applying selections alongside the input.

templates.name: TokenizerIcon
templates.description: Tokenizer with a leading search icon to visually reinforce the search behavior.

templates.name: TokenizerMaxEntries
templates.description: Tokenizer with a maximum selection limit. The input hides automatically when the limit is reached, preventing further additions.

templates.name: TokenizerOverflow
templates.description: Tokenizer with overflow truncation when unfocused. Inline mode pushes content down on expand; layer mode overlays without shifting layout. Overflow modes apply to the inline field.

templates.name: TokenizerStates
templates.description: Tokenizer in disabled, error, warning, and success states. Use to communicate validation feedback or lock a selection from editing.

templates.name: ToolbarBulkActions
templates.description: A compact toolbar with the muted variant for showing bulk selection actions. Use when the user selects multiple items in a list or table and needs quick access to batch operations.

templates.name: ToolbarCardHeader
templates.description: A toolbar as a card header with a left-aligned title and icon actions on the right. Use Toolbar instead of LayoutHeader when your card header has interactive actions; Toolbar adds start/end slot layout, keyboard navigation, and automatic size cascading. If the header is just a title with no actions, a LayoutHeader or Section is enough.

templates.name: ToolbarSizes
templates.description: Small, medium, and large toolbars side by side. The size prop cascades to child buttons and inputs automatically. Use small in dense UIs like cards, medium for most cases, and large for spacious layouts.

templates.name: ToolbarWithTabs
templates.description: A toolbar with tabs in the start slot and an action button at the end. Use as a card or section header when content is split into tabs with a primary action alongside.

templates.name: ToolbarTableFilter
templates.description: Filter bar above a table: a search box leads the row, each field beside it is a closed trigger that doubles as its own filter chip — the bare field name unset, the whole clause once set — and the clauses fold from the end into a count as the row narrows, followed by a live result count, a clear all, and a column picker. Use to search, filter, and narrow flat rows of records such as jobs, orders, tickets, or users.

templates.name: ToolbarThreeSlot
templates.description: A toolbar with start, center, and end content using the three-column grid layout. Use when you need a centered title or heading with navigation and actions on either side.

templates.name: TooltipActionBarTooltips
templates.description: Tooltips on an action button bar with contextual descriptions.

templates.name: TooltipHookUsage
templates.description: Tooltip using the useTooltip hook for programmatic control.

templates.name: TooltipInlineTextTooltips
templates.description: Tooltips on inline text terms for definitions.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuShowcase
templates.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenu with items and a featured card in the mega menu panel.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuBasic
templates.description: A mega menu trigger inside a TopNav that opens a panel of rich link items. Use when a navigation section has multiple destinations worth describing.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCardShowcase
templates.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCard with a title, description, and CTA link inside a mega menu.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuFeaturedCardBasic
templates.description: A promotional card with a title, description, and call-to-action link. Pass it to the featured slot of a TopNavMegaMenu to highlight announcements.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuItemShowcase
templates.description: Demonstrates TopNavMegaMenuItem with icons, titles, and descriptions inside a mega menu.

templates.name: TopNavMegaMenuItemBasic
templates.description: Rich link items with an icon, title, and description. Use inside the items slot of a TopNavMegaMenu to describe each destination.

templates.name: TopNavMenuShowcase
templates.description: Demonstrates TopNavMenu with a hover-triggered dropdown containing items with icons and descriptions.

templates.name: TopNavMenuBasic
templates.description: A dropdown menu inside a TopNav built from an items array with icons and descriptions. Use to group related destinations under a single trigger.

templates.description: Typeahead with a capped dropdown showing at most three results.
